Identifiability and Stability of Generative Drifting with Companion-Elliptic Kernel Families

Lee Hak Geun ††thanks: Korea Advanced Institute of Science & Technology (KAIST).
Abstract

This paper analyzes identifiability and stability for the drifting field underlying distributional matching in the Generative Drifting framework of Deng et al. [1]. First, we introduce the class of companion-elliptic kernels, which includes the Laplace kernel and is characterized by a second-order elliptic coupling between each kernel κ\kappa in this class and its companion function η\eta. For each kernel in this class and each pair of Borel probability measures, we prove that the drifting field vanishes if and only if the two probability measures are equal. We further show that this class consists precisely of Gaussian kernels and Matérn kernels with ν≥1/2\nu\geq 1/2. Second, by constructing counterexamples, we exhibit sequences for which mass escapes to infinity while the field tends to zero; in particular, control of the field norm alone does not guarantee weak convergence. Nevertheless, we prove that the only possible mode of failure is confined to the one-dimensional ray {c​p:0≤c≤1}\{c\,p:0\leq c\leq 1\}. Consequently, weak convergence can be restored by imposing an asymptotic lower bound on the intrinsic overlap scalar, a linear observable defined by the kernel and the target measure.

1 Introduction

1.1 Theoretical point of departure

Deng et al. [1] adopt the viewpoint that generative modeling is the problem of learning the pushforward of a prior distribution. More precisely, given a prior law pεp_{\varepsilon} and a generator fθ:ℝC→ℝDf_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{C}\to\mathbb{R}^{D}, the model law is defined by

qθ=fθ​#​pε.q_{\theta}=f_{\theta\#}p_{\varepsilon}.

In this setting, diffusion models [21, 22] and flow matching [23] implement complex pushforwards through multi-step inference-time updates. By contrast, drifting keeps inference single-step and instead evolves the pushforward law itself during training. Accordingly, Deng et al. [1] describe the training process as producing a sequence of parameters θ0,θ1,θ2,…\theta_{0},\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\dots together with a corresponding chain of laws

qi=[fθi]#​pε,q_{i}=[f_{\theta_{i}}]_{\#}p_{\varepsilon},

whose evolution is described directly at the level of distributions.

To formalize this perspective, Deng et al. [1] introduce a vector field

Vp,q:ℝd→ℝdV_{p,q}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}

that depends on the target law pp and the current law qq. Ideally, a generated sample xi=fθi​(ε)∼qix_{i}=f_{\theta_{i}}(\varepsilon)\sim q_{i} should move according to

xi+1≈xi+Vp,qi​(xi),x_{i+1}\approx x_{i}+V_{p,q_{i}}(x_{i}),

and the accumulated sample-level drift then pushes the training-time pushforward qiq_{i} toward pp. Once training has converged, the two distributions should coincide, which requires the drifting field to vanish. In their theory, distributional matching is therefore expressed as a zero-drift equilibrium. Deng et al. [1] propose a drifting field satisfying the antisymmetry relation

Vp,q​(x)=−Vq,p​(x),V_{p,q}(x)=-V_{q,p}(x),

which yields

p=q⟹Vp,q≡0.p=q\Longrightarrow V_{p,q}\equiv 0.

The problem left open by Deng et al. [1] is precisely the converse implication: does Vp,q≡0V_{p,q}\equiv 0 force p=qp=q?

Deng et al. [1] regard the drifting field as a general kernelized interaction. At the most abstract level, one may write

Vp,q​(x)=𝔼y+∼p,y−∼q​[K⁡(x,y+,y−)],V_{p,q}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{y^{+}\sim p,\,y^{-}\sim q}[K(x,y^{+},y^{-})],

where y+y^{+} is a positive sample from the data distribution pp and y−y^{-} is a negative sample from the model distribution qq. A canonical instance of the drifting field is a mean-shift-type attraction–repulsion structure [24, 25]. Specifically, for a positive kernel kk, set

Vp+​(x):=∫k⁡(x,y)​(y−x)​p​(𝑑y)∫k⁡(x,y)​p​(𝑑y),Vq−​(x):=∫k⁡(x,y)​(y−x)​q​(𝑑y)∫k⁡(x,y)​q​(𝑑y),V_{p}^{+}(x):=\frac{\int k(x,y)(y-x)\,p(dy)}{\int k(x,y)\,p(dy)},\qquad V_{q}^{-}(x):=\frac{\int k(x,y)(y-x)\,q(dy)}{\int k(x,y)\,q(dy)},

and

Vp,q​(x)=Vp+​(x)−Vq−​(x).V_{p,q}(x)=V_{p}^{+}(x)-V_{q}^{-}(x). (1.1)

Equation (1.1) is interpreted as a field that attracts samples toward the local barycenter induced by pp and repels them from the local barycenter induced by qq. Deng et al. [1] also introduce an equivalent representation

Vp,q​(x)=1up​(x)​uq​(x)​∬k⁡(x,y+)​k​(x,y−)​(y+−y−)​p​(d​y+)​q​(d​y−),ur​(x):=∫k⁡(x,y)​r​(𝑑y).V_{p,q}(x)=\frac{1}{u_{p}(x)u_{q}(x)}\iint k(x,y^{+})k(x,y^{-})(y^{+}-y^{-})\,p(dy^{+})q(dy^{-}),\qquad u_{r}(x):=\int k(x,y)\,r(dy).

1.2 Problem formulation

We now specialize the preceding general framework to the raw-space Laplace setting. Specifically, let

kτ(x,y)=e−‖x−y‖/τ,τ>0,k_{\tau}(x,y)=e^{-\left\lVert x-y\right\rVert/\tau},\qquad\tau>0,

and, for a probability measure rr on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, define

ar​(x)=mr​(x)ur​(x),ur​(x):=∫kτ​(x,y)​r​(𝑑y),mr​(x):=∫y​kτ​(x,y)​r​(𝑑y).a_{r}(x)=\frac{m_{r}(x)}{u_{r}(x)},\qquad u_{r}(x):=\int k_{\tau}(x,y)\,r(dy),\qquad m_{r}(x):=\int y\,k_{\tau}(x,y)\,r(dy).

Then the raw-space drifting field is

Vp,q​(x):=ap​(x)−aq​(x).V_{p,q}(x):=a_{p}(x)-a_{q}(x).

This paper addresses two questions.

  1. (Q1)

    Field identifiability. Does the implication

    Vp,q≡0⟹p=qV_{p,q}\equiv 0\Longrightarrow p=q

    hold? This is the problem posed by Deng et al. [1].

  2. (Q2)

    Field stability. In which topology, and with what additional scalar observable, does

    Vp,qn→0V_{p,q_{n}}\to 0

    force qn⇒pq_{n}\Rightarrow p?

Our results are as follows. For the Laplace kernel, the implication in (Q1) holds for the full class of Borel probability measures. Moreover, the same mechanism extends to the entire translation-invariant companion-elliptic kernel family. For (Q2), the corresponding stability statement fails without an additional observable: neither locally uniform (compact-open) control nor global L∞L^{\infty} control implies weak convergence. However, within the companion-elliptic class, the only possible limiting defect lies on the one-dimensional ray {c​p:0≤c≤1}\{c\,p:0\leq c\leq 1\}. Adding a single scalar observable that separates the target point from all other points on this ray restores weak convergence.

2 Related work

Our starting point is the work of Deng et al. [1], which introduced the drifting field and documented its empirical behavior. Several recent works have clarified related aspects of drifting. Li and Zhu reinterpreted drifting through a long–short flow-map factorization [14]. Lai et al. showed that, for the Gaussian kernel, drifting coincides exactly with a score mismatch and that, in an appropriate asymptotic regime, it provides a controlled approximation in the Laplace-kernel setting [13]. Turan and Ovsjanikov derived a Gaussian-kernel score-matching identity and developed its spectral and variational consequences [20]. These score-based reinterpretations connect directly to the classical principle of score matching [26]. Cao, Wei, and Liu placed drifting in a broader Wasserstein gradient-flow framework for KDE-approximated divergences [2, 9], while explicitly noting that the Laplace kernel does not belong to their kernel class [9]. He et al. proved identifiability for a Sinkhorn-normalized two-sided variant, thereby highlighting the gap between one-sided and two-sided formulations [12]. Within the one-sided raw drifting formulation of Deng et al. [1], the present paper establishes identifiability on the full space of Borel probability measures and characterizes the stability obstruction caused by mass escape. Our results cover both the Laplace kernel and the companion-elliptic kernel family that contains it.

4 Field identifiability on the full class of Borel probability measures

This section answers (Q1). We prove that, for arbitrary Borel probability measures p,qp,q on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, the identity Vp,q≡0V_{p,q}\equiv 0 implies p=qp=q.

and integrating both sides gives (4.4). ∎

Theorem 4.2 (Renormalization for continuity equations with locally Lipschitz velocity fields).

Let b:ℝd→ℝdb:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} be locally Lipschitz, and let

ρ∈Lloc∞​(ℝt,L1​(ℝd)∩L∞​(ℝd))\rho\in L^{\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}\bigl(\mathbb{R}_{t};L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\bigr)

be a distributional solution of

∂tρ+∇⋅(b​ρ)=0on ​ℝt×ℝd.\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot(b\rho)=0\qquad\text{on }\mathbb{R}_{t}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Here, by local Lipschitz regularity,

b∈Wloc1,∞​(ℝd,ℝd),∇⋅b:=tr⁡(D​b)∈Lloc∞​(ℝd).b\in W^{1,\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{R}^{d}),\qquad\nabla\cdot b:=\operatorname{tr}(Db)\in L^{\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

Let β∈C1​(ℝ)\beta\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}) satisfy β⁡(0)=0\beta(0)=0, assume that β′\beta^{\prime} is bounded, and assume that

z⟼z​β′​(z)−β⁡(z)z\longmapsto z\beta^{\prime}(z)-\beta(z)

is bounded on ℝ\mathbb{R}. Then the following renormalized identity holds in the sense of distributions on ℝt×ℝd\mathbb{R}_{t}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}:

∂tβ(ρ)+∇⋅(bβ(ρ))+(β′(ρ)ρ−β(ρ))∇⋅b=0.\partial_{t}\beta(\rho)+\nabla\cdot\bigl(b\,\beta(\rho)\bigr)+\bigl(\beta^{\prime}(\rho)\rho-\beta(\rho)\bigr)\nabla\cdot b=0.

In particular, for

βε​(z):=z2+ε2−ε,\beta_{\varepsilon}(z):=\sqrt{z^{2}+\varepsilon^{2}}-\varepsilon,

taking the limit ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0 gives, in the distributional sense,

∂t|ρ|+∇⋅(b​|ρ|)=0.\partial_{t}|\rho|+\nabla\cdot(b|\rho|)=0.
Proof.

A proof is given in Appendix A. This theorem is also a special case of the classical renormalization theory of DiPerna–Lions and Ambrosio [3, 10]. ∎

Lemma 4.3 (Mass conservation for renormalized integrable fluxes).

Let b:ℝd→ℝdb:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} be locally Lipschitz, and let

ρ∈Lloc∞​(ℝt,L1​(ℝd)∩L∞​(ℝd))\rho\in L^{\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}\bigl(\mathbb{R}_{t};L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\bigr)

be a distributional solution of

∂tρ+∇⋅(b​ρ)=0on ​ℝt×ℝd.\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot(b\rho)=0\qquad\text{on }\mathbb{R}_{t}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Assume additionally that

b​ρ∈Lloc∞​(ℝt,L1​(ℝd,ℝd)).b\rho\in L^{\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}\bigl(\mathbb{R}_{t};L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{R}^{d})\bigr).

By Theorem 4.2, |ρ||\rho| is a distributional solution of

∂t|ρ|+∇⋅(b​|ρ|)=0.\partial_{t}|\rho|+\nabla\cdot(b|\rho|)=0.

Lloc∞​(ℝt,L1​(ℝd,ℝd)).L^{\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}\bigl(\mathbb{R}_{t};L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{R}^{d})\bigr).

Choose χ∈Cc∞​(ℝd)\chi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) such that 0≤χ≤10\leq\chi\leq 1, χ≡1\chi\equiv 1 on B1​(0)B_{1}(0), and supp⁡(χ)⊂B2​(0)\supp(\chi)\subset B_{2}(0), and define

χR​(x):=χ⁡(x/R).\chi_{R}(x):=\chi(x/R).

Let φ∈Cc∞​(ℝ)\varphi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) be arbitrary, and choose a compact interval I⊂ℝI\subset\mathbb{R} such that supp⁡(φ)⊂I\supp(\varphi)\subset I. Testing the equation for |ρ||\rho| against φ⁡(t)​χR​(x)\varphi(t)\chi_{R}(x) gives

∫ℝφ′​(t)​∫ℝdχR​(x)|ρ⁡(t,x)​|d​x​𝑑t+∫ℝφ⁡(t)​∫ℝd∇χR​(x)⋅b⁡(x)|​ρ​(t,x)|d​x​𝑑t=0.\int_{\mathbb{R}}\varphi^{\prime}(t)\!\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\chi_{R}(x)|\rho(t,x)|\,dx\,dt+\int_{\mathbb{R}}\varphi(t)\!\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\nabla\chi_{R}(x)\cdot b(x)|\rho(t,x)|\,dx\,dt=0. (4.10)

We now show that the flux term tends to 00 as R→∞R\to\infty. Indeed, since supp(∇χR)⊂{R≤‖x‖≤2R}\supp(\nabla\chi_{R})\subset\{R\leq\left\lVert x\right\rVert\leq 2R\} and ‖∇χR‖∞≤C/R\|\nabla\chi_{R}\|_{\infty}\leq C/R,

|∫ℝφ⁡(t)​∫ℝd∇χR​(x)⋅b⁡(x)​|ρ⁡(t,x)|​dx​dt|\displaystyle\left|\int_{\mathbb{R}}\varphi(t)\!\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\nabla\chi_{R}(x)\cdot b(x)|\rho(t,x)|\,dx\,dt\right| ≤‖φ‖L∞​(ℝ)​∫I∫ℝd|∇χR​(x)|​|b⁡(x)​ρ​(t,x)|​𝑑x​𝑑t\displaystyle\leq\|\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})}\int_{I}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|\nabla\chi_{R}(x)|\,|b(x)\rho(t,x)|\,dx\,dt (4.11)
≤C​‖φ‖L∞​(ℝ)R​∫I‖b​ρ​(t,⋅)‖L1​(ℝd,ℝd)​dt.\displaystyle\leq\frac{C\|\varphi\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})}}{R}\int_{I}\|b\rho(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{R}^{d})}\,dt.

Because b​ρ∈Lloc∞​(ℝt,Lx1)b\rho\in L^{\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}_{t};L^{1}_{x}), the last integral in (4.11) is finite, and the entire right-hand side is O⁡(R−1)O(R^{-1}). Hence

∫ℝφ⁡(t)​∫ℝd∇χR​(x)⋅b⁡(x)|ρ⁡(t,x)|d​x​𝑑t⟶0.\int_{\mathbb{R}}\varphi(t)\!\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\nabla\chi_{R}(x)\cdot b(x)|\rho(t,x)|\,dx\,dt\longrightarrow 0. (4.12)

0≤∫ℝdχR​(x)​|ρ⁡(t,x)|​𝑑x≤‖ρ⁡(t,⋅)‖L1​(ℝd),0\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\chi_{R}(x)|\rho(t,x)|\,dx\leq\|\rho(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})},

Taking the limits (4.12) and (4.13) in (4.10), we obtain

∫ℝφ′​(t)​(∫ℝd|ρ⁡(t,x)|​𝑑x)​𝑑t=0(∀φ∈Cc∞​(ℝ)).\int_{\mathbb{R}}\varphi^{\prime}(t)\left(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|\rho(t,x)|\,dx\right)dt=0\qquad(\forall\varphi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R})).

Thus the distributional derivative of t↦‖ρ⁡(t,⋅)‖L1t\mapsto\|\rho(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{1}} is zero, which means that the function is distributionally constant. This proves the claim. ∎

5 Beyond the Laplace kernel: identifiability and classification

In Section 4, we established that, for the Laplace kernel,

Vp,q≡0⟹p=q.V_{p,q}\equiv 0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad p=q.

Which property of the Laplace kernel makes this conclusion possible? Is it the specific exponential form, or does a more structural mechanism lie behind it? This question naturally splits into two parts.

  • •

    Does the conclusion proved above for the Laplace kernel hold in a broader class of translation-invariant kernels?

  • •

    If it does, which concrete kernels possess this structure?

This section answers both questions. We introduce a local condition under which a kernel κ\kappa and its companion η\eta are coupled through a second-order elliptic operator λ0​I−λ1​Δ\lambda_{0}I-\lambda_{1}\Delta. First, field identifiability holds under this condition (Theorem 5.6). Moreover, the same condition completely determines the kernel: the kernels in the companion-elliptic class are precisely Gaussian kernels and Matérn kernels with ν≥12\nu\geq\tfrac{1}{2} (Theorem 5.10). Since the Laplace kernel is a special case of the Matérn family with ν=12\nu=\tfrac{1}{2} [8, 18, 19], the result of Section 4 fits naturally into a broader classification.

Definition 5.1 (Translation-invariant drift).

Let κ:ℝd→(0,∞)\kappa:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to(0,\infty) be a Borel function, and let rr be a Borel probability measure on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Define

urκ​(x):=∫ℝdκ⁡(x−y)​r​(𝑑y)∈(0,∞],u_{r}^{\kappa}(x):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\kappa(x-y)\,r(dy)\in(0,\infty],

and define the barycenter domain by

Drκ:={x∈ℝd:urκ​(x)<∞​and​∫ℝd‖y−x‖​κ​(x−y)​r​(𝑑y)<∞}.D_{r}^{\kappa}:=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:u_{r}^{\kappa}(x)<\infty\ \text{and}\ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert\,\kappa(x-y)\,r(dy)<\infty\right\}.

For x∈Drκx\in D_{r}^{\kappa}, define the centered kernel moment by

wrκ​(x):=∫ℝd(y−x)​κ​(x−y)​r​(𝑑y),w_{r}^{\kappa}(x):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}(y-x)\,\kappa(x-y)\,r(dy),

and the normalized local barycenter by

arκ​(x):=x+wrκ​(x)urκ​(x).a_{r}^{\kappa}(x):=x+\frac{w_{r}^{\kappa}(x)}{u_{r}^{\kappa}(x)}.

If, additionally,

∫ℝd‖y‖​κ​(x−y)​r​(𝑑y)<∞,\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left\lVert y\right\rVert\,\kappa(x-y)\,r(dy)<\infty,

we also write

mrκ​(x):=∫ℝdy​κ​(x−y)​r​(𝑑y),m_{r}^{\kappa}(x):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}y\,\kappa(x-y)\,r(dy),

in which case

wrκ​(x)=mrκ​(x)−x​urκ​(x),arκ​(x)=mrκ​(x)urκ​(x).w_{r}^{\kappa}(x)=m_{r}^{\kappa}(x)-x\,u_{r}^{\kappa}(x),\qquad a_{r}^{\kappa}(x)=\frac{m_{r}^{\kappa}(x)}{u_{r}^{\kappa}(x)}.

For two Borel probability measures p,qp,q, the associated drift field is the map defined on

Dp,qκ:=Dpκ∩DqκD_{p,q}^{\kappa}:=D_{p}^{\kappa}\cap D_{q}^{\kappa}

by

Vp,qκ​(x):=apκ​(x)−aqκ​(x).V_{p,q}^{\kappa}(x):=a_{p}^{\kappa}(x)-a_{q}^{\kappa}(x).
Assumption 5.2 (Companion-elliptic kernel class).

Let κ:ℝd→(0,∞)\kappa:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to(0,\infty). We impose the following assumptions.

  1. (CE1)

    κ∈C⁡(ℝd)∩L1​(ℝd)∩W1,∞​(ℝd)\kappa\in C(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

  2. (CE2)

    There exist constants c1,c2,λ0>0c_{1},c_{2},\lambda_{0}>0 and λ1≥0\lambda_{1}\geq 0, together with η∈C2​(ℝd)\eta\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), such that η\eta is strictly positive on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d},

    η,∇η∈C0​(ℝd)∩L1​(ℝd)∩L∞​(ℝd),∇2η∈L∞​(ℝd),\eta,\nabla\eta\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\qquad\nabla^{2}\eta\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),

    and

    ∇η(z)=−zc1κ(z),(λ0I−λ1Δ)η(z)=c2κ(z)(z∈ℝd).\nabla\eta(z)=-\frac{z}{c_{1}}\,\kappa(z),\qquad(\lambda_{0}I-\lambda_{1}\Delta)\eta(z)=c_{2}\kappa(z)\qquad(z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}). (5.1)

This assumption captures, in abstract form, the two identities used in the proof of Lemma 4.1 for the Laplace kernel. Specifically, for kτ(z)=e−‖z‖/τk_{\tau}(z)=e^{-\left\lVert z\right\rVert/\tau} and ητ(z)=(1+‖z‖/τ)e−‖z‖/τ\eta_{\tau}(z)=(1+\left\lVert z\right\rVert/\tau)e^{-\left\lVert z\right\rVert/\tau}, equations (4.7) and (4.9) show that the Laplace kernel satisfies the structure in (5.1). Convolving these two identities with a probability measure rr yields (4.1) and (4.2), which shows that (4.7) and (4.9) constitute the central mechanism in the proof. Condition (5.1) is introduced precisely in order to extend this mechanism to a general class of translation-invariant kernels.

Lemma 5.3 (Vanishing at infinity for uniformly continuous L1L^{1} functions).

If f:ℝd→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} is uniformly continuous and f∈L1​(ℝd)f\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), then f∈C0​(ℝd)f\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

Proof.

Suppose, to the contrary, that f∉C0​(ℝd)f\notin C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Then there exist ε>0\varepsilon>0 and a sequence ‖xn‖→∞\left\lVert x_{n}\right\rVert\to\infty such that

|f⁡(xn)|≥ε(n≥1).\left\lvert f(x_{n})\right\rvert\geq\varepsilon\qquad(n\geq 1).

By uniform continuity, there exists r>0r>0 such that, whenever ‖y−xn‖<r\left\lVert y-x_{n}\right\rVert<r,

|f⁡(y)−f⁡(xn)|<ε2.\left\lvert f(y)-f(x_{n})\right\rvert<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}.

Therefore |f⁡(y)|≥ε/2\left\lvert f(y)\right\rvert\geq\varepsilon/2 on B⁡(xn,r)B(x_{n},r). Passing to a subsequence, we may arrange that the balls B⁡(xn,r)B(x_{n},r) are pairwise disjoint. Hence

∫ℝd|f⁡(y)|​𝑑y≥∑n∫B⁡(xn,r)|f⁡(y)|​𝑑y≥∑nε2|B⁡(0,r)|=∞,\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left\lvert f(y)\right\rvert\,dy\geq\sum_{n}\int_{B(x_{n},r)}\left\lvert f(y)\right\rvert\,dy\geq\sum_{n}\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\,|B(0,r)|=\infty,

which contradicts f∈L1​(ℝd)f\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Thus f∈C0​(ℝd)f\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). ∎

Lemma 5.4 (Companion identities in the companion-elliptic class).

Assume Assumption 5.2. Let rr be a Borel probability measure on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and set

Ψrκ:=η∗r.\Psi_{r}^{\kappa}:=\eta*r.

Then Drκ=ℝdD_{r}^{\kappa}=\mathbb{R}^{d}, and urκu_{r}^{\kappa}, mrκm_{r}^{\kappa}, and arκa_{r}^{\kappa} are well-defined and continuous on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Moreover, Ψrκ∈C2​(ℝd)\Psi_{r}^{\kappa}\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), Ψrκ>0\Psi_{r}^{\kappa}>0, and

urκ,Ψrκ,∇Ψrκ∈C0​(ℝd)∩L1​(ℝd).u_{r}^{\kappa},\ \Psi_{r}^{\kappa},\ \nabla\Psi_{r}^{\kappa}\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

Furthermore, the following identities hold:

mrκ​(x)−x​urκ​(x)\displaystyle m_{r}^{\kappa}(x)-x\,u_{r}^{\kappa}(x) =c1∇Ψrκ(x),\displaystyle=c_{1}\nabla\Psi_{r}^{\kappa}(x), (5.2)
(λ0​I−λ1​Δ)​Ψrκ​(x)\displaystyle(\lambda_{0}I-\lambda_{1}\Delta)\Psi_{r}^{\kappa}(x) =c2​urκ​(x),\displaystyle=c_{2}u_{r}^{\kappa}(x), (5.3)

Proof.

Since κ∈W1,∞​(ℝd)\kappa\in W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), it follows that κ∈L∞​(ℝd)\kappa\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), and hence

urκ​(x)≤‖κ‖L∞<∞(x∈ℝd).u_{r}^{\kappa}(x)\leq\left\lVert\kappa\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}}<\infty\qquad(x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}).

Also, by (5.1),

supz∈ℝd‖z‖​κ​(z)=c1​supz∈ℝd‖∇η​(z)‖<∞.\sup_{z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left\lVert z\right\rVert\,\kappa(z)=c_{1}\sup_{z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left\lVert\nabla\eta(z)\right\rVert<\infty.

Therefore

∫ℝd‖y−x‖​κ​(x−y)​r​(𝑑y)≤supz∈ℝd‖z‖​κ​(z)<∞(x∈ℝd),\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert\,\kappa(x-y)\,r(dy)\leq\sup_{z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left\lVert z\right\rVert\,\kappa(z)<\infty\qquad(x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}),

so Drκ=ℝdD_{r}^{\kappa}=\mathbb{R}^{d}. In particular,

and hence mrκm_{r}^{\kappa} and arκa_{r}^{\kappa} are globally well-defined. Since η∈C2​(ℝd)\eta\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and its first and second derivatives are bounded, differentiation under the integral sign is justified for the finite measure rr. Thus Ψrκ∈C2​(ℝd)\Psi_{r}^{\kappa}\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and Ψrκ>0\Psi_{r}^{\kappa}>0.

From (5.1),

∇xη​(x−y)=−x−yc1​κ​(x−y)=y−xc1​κ​(x−y),\nabla_{x}\eta(x-y)=-\frac{x-y}{c_{1}}\,\kappa(x-y)=\frac{y-x}{c_{1}}\,\kappa(x-y),

By Assumption 5.2, κ∈W1,∞​(ℝd)\kappa\in W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), and we take κ\kappa to be its continuous representative. Hence it is globally Lipschitz, in particular uniformly continuous. Since κ∈L1​(ℝd)\kappa\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), Lemma 5.3 gives κ∈C0​(ℝd)\kappa\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Applying Lemma 3.4 to κ\kappa and the probability measure rr gives

urκ=κ∗r∈C0​(ℝd)∩L1​(ℝd).u_{r}^{\kappa}=\kappa*r\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

Assume Assumption 5.2. Then κ^∈C1​(ℝd)\widehat{\kappa}\in C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and

Theorem 5.6 (Field identifiability in the companion-elliptic class).

Assume Assumption 5.2. Then, for arbitrary Borel probability measures p,qp,q on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, the drift field Vp,qκV_{p,q}^{\kappa} is well-defined on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and

Vp,qκ≡0⟹p=q.V_{p,q}^{\kappa}\equiv 0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad p=q.
Proof.

Let ur,mr,ar,Ψru_{r},m_{r},a_{r},\Psi_{r} denote the functions corresponding to the fixed kernel κ\kappa, and assume Vp,qκ≡0V_{p,q}^{\kappa}\equiv 0. Then

ap=aq=:a.a_{p}=a_{q}=:a.

Define

b⁡(x):=a⁡(x)−xc1​c2.b(x):=\frac{a(x)-x}{c_{1}c_{2}}.

∇Ψp=b⁡(λ0​I−λ1​Δ)​Ψp,∇Ψq=b⁡(λ0​I−λ1​Δ)​Ψq.\nabla\Psi_{p}=b\,(\lambda_{0}I-\lambda_{1}\Delta)\Psi_{p},\qquad\nabla\Psi_{q}=b\,(\lambda_{0}I-\lambda_{1}\Delta)\Psi_{q}. (5.8)

Set

J:=Ψq∇Ψp−Ψp∇Ψq.J:=\Psi_{q}\nabla\Psi_{p}-\Psi_{p}\nabla\Psi_{q}.

If λ1=0\lambda_{1}=0, then

J=b⁡(λ0​Ψq​Ψp−λ0​Ψp​Ψq)=0.J=b\bigl(\lambda_{0}\Psi_{q}\Psi_{p}-\lambda_{0}\Psi_{p}\Psi_{q}\bigr)=0.

On the other hand, if λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0, define

s:=∇⋅J=Ψq​Δ​Ψp−Ψp​Δ​Ψq.s:=\nabla\cdot J=\Psi_{q}\Delta\Psi_{p}-\Psi_{p}\Delta\Psi_{q}. (5.9)

Multiplying the two identities in (5.8) by Ψq\Psi_{q} and Ψp\Psi_{p}, respectively, and subtracting, we obtain

J\displaystyle J =Ψq∇Ψp−Ψp∇Ψq\displaystyle=\Psi_{q}\nabla\Psi_{p}-\Psi_{p}\nabla\Psi_{q} (5.10)
=b​Ψq​(λ0​I−λ1​Δ)​Ψp−b​Ψp​(λ0​I−λ1​Δ)​Ψq\displaystyle=b\,\Psi_{q}(\lambda_{0}I-\lambda_{1}\Delta)\Psi_{p}-b\,\Psi_{p}(\lambda_{0}I-\lambda_{1}\Delta)\Psi_{q}
=b⁡(λ0​Ψq​Ψp−λ1​Ψq​Δ​Ψp−λ0​Ψp​Ψq+λ1​Ψp​Δ​Ψq)\displaystyle=b\Bigl(\lambda_{0}\Psi_{q}\Psi_{p}-\lambda_{1}\Psi_{q}\Delta\Psi_{p}-\lambda_{0}\Psi_{p}\Psi_{q}+\lambda_{1}\Psi_{p}\Delta\Psi_{q}\Bigr)
=−λ1​b​(Ψq​Δ​Ψp−Ψp​Δ​Ψq)=−λ1​b​s.\displaystyle=-\lambda_{1}b\,(\Psi_{q}\Delta\Psi_{p}-\Psi_{p}\Delta\Psi_{q})=-\lambda_{1}b\,s.

Thus the terms involving λ0\lambda_{0} cancel exactly, as shown in (5.10). Combining s=∇⋅Js=\nabla\cdot J with (5.10) gives

s=∇⋅(−λ1​b​s),s=\nabla\cdot(-\lambda_{1}b\,s),

and hence

s+λ1∇⋅(bs)=0s+\lambda_{1}\nabla\cdot(bs)=0 (5.11)

in the distributional sense.

We now check the integrability needed when λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0. By Lemma 5.4, Ψr∈L∞∩L1\Psi_{r}\in L^{\infty}\cap L^{1} and ∇Ψr∈L∞∩L1\nabla\Psi_{r}\in L^{\infty}\cap L^{1}, so

J∈L1​(ℝd,ℝd).J\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{R}^{d}).

Also, by (5.3),

Δ​Ψr=λ0​Ψr−c2​urλ1(λ1>0),\Delta\Psi_{r}=\frac{\lambda_{0}\Psi_{r}-c_{2}u_{r}}{\lambda_{1}}\qquad(\lambda_{1}>0),

so

s=c2λ1​(Ψp​uq−Ψq​up).s=\frac{c_{2}}{\lambda_{1}}\bigl(\Psi_{p}u_{q}-\Psi_{q}u_{p}\bigr).

Since ur∈L1∩L∞u_{r}\in L^{1}\cap L^{\infty} and Ψr∈L1∩L∞\Psi_{r}\in L^{1}\cap L^{\infty},

s∈L1​(ℝd)∩L∞​(ℝd).s\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

When λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0, we verify that bb is locally Lipschitz. From (5.4),

b=∇Ψqc2​uq.b=\frac{\nabla\Psi_{q}}{c_{2}u_{q}}.

The numerator ∇Ψq\nabla\Psi_{q} is locally Lipschitz because Ψq∈C2\Psi_{q}\in C^{2}. The denominator uq=κ∗qu_{q}=\kappa*q is globally Lipschitz since κ∈W1,∞​(ℝd)\kappa\in W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), and on each compact set it has a strictly positive minimum by the positivity of κ\kappa and the continuity of uqu_{q}. Therefore the quotient bb is locally Lipschitz.

Still assuming λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0, define

ρ⁡(t,x):=et/λ1​s​(x).\rho(t,x):=e^{t/\lambda_{1}}s(x).

By (5.11), ρ\rho is a distributional solution of

∂tρ+∇⋅(b​ρ)=0on ​ℝt×ℝd.\partial_{t}\rho+\nabla\cdot(b\rho)=0\qquad\text{on }\mathbb{R}_{t}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Moreover,

ρ∈Lloc∞​(ℝt,L1​(ℝd)∩L∞​(ℝd)),b​ρ=−et/λ1λ1​J∈Lloc∞​(ℝt,L1​(ℝd,ℝd)).\rho\in L^{\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}\bigl(\mathbb{R}_{t};L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\bigr),\qquad b\rho=-\frac{e^{t/\lambda_{1}}}{\lambda_{1}}J\in L^{\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}\bigl(\mathbb{R}_{t};L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{R}^{d})\bigr).

‖ρ⁡(t,⋅)‖L1​(ℝd)=et/λ1​‖s‖L1​(ℝd).\|\rho(t,\cdot)\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}=e^{t/\lambda_{1}}\|s\|_{L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}. (5.12)

It follows that ‖s‖L1=0\|s\|_{L^{1}}=0. Thus s=0s=0 almost everywhere. Since (5.9) and Ψp,Ψq∈C2​(ℝd)\Psi_{p},\Psi_{q}\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) imply s∈C⁡(ℝd)s\in C(\mathbb{R}^{d}), we have s≡0s\equiv 0. When λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0, (5.10) gives J=−λ1​b​sJ=-\lambda_{1}bs, and hence J≡0J\equiv 0.

Consequently, in either case J≡0J\equiv 0. Since Ψq>0\Psi_{q}>0 everywhere,

∇(ΨpΨq)=JΨq2=0.\nabla\!\left(\frac{\Psi_{p}}{\Psi_{q}}\right)=\frac{J}{\Psi_{q}^{2}}=0.

By the connectedness of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, there exists c>0c>0 such that

Ψp=c​Ψq.\Psi_{p}=c\,\Psi_{q}.

Applying (5.3), we obtain

up=c​uq.u_{p}=c\,u_{q}.

For each r∈{p,q}r\in\{p,q\},

∫ℝdur​(x)​𝑑x=∫ℝdκ⁡(z)​𝑑z.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}u_{r}(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\kappa(z)\,dz.

Integrating both sides yields c=1c=1. Therefore up=uqu_{p}=u_{q}. Taking the Fourier transform, we obtain

κ^​(ξ)​(p^​(ξ)−q^​(ξ))=0(ξ∈ℝd).\widehat{\kappa}(\xi)\bigl(\widehat{p}(\xi)-\widehat{q}(\xi)\bigr)=0\qquad(\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{d}).

By Lemma 5.5, κ^​(ξ)>0\widehat{\kappa}(\xi)>0 for every ξ\xi, so p^=q^\widehat{p}=\widehat{q}. Applying Lemma 3.2 to the finite signed measure p−qp-q proves p=qp=q. ∎

Theorem 5.6 answers the first of the two questions posed above, namely, field identifiability. For this result to have substantive content, however, one must verify that sufficiently many kernels satisfy the hypothesis. If only the Laplace kernel belonged to this class, the framework would offer little beyond the case already treated.

Proposition 5.7 (The Gaussian kernel satisfies the companion-elliptic hypothesis).

For σ>0\sigma>0, define

κσ​(z):=exp⁡(−‖z‖22​σ2).\kappa_{\sigma}(z):=\exp\!\left(-\frac{\left\lVert z\right\rVert^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right).

Then κσ\kappa_{\sigma} satisfies Assumption 5.2.

Proof.

The Gaussian function κσ\kappa_{\sigma} is C∞C^{\infty}, strictly positive, and belongs to L1​(ℝd)L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Its first derivatives are products of polynomials and Gaussians, and hence are bounded. Therefore

κσ∈C⁡(ℝd)∩L1​(ℝd)∩W1,∞​(ℝd).\kappa_{\sigma}\in C(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

Set ησ:=κσ\eta_{\sigma}:=\kappa_{\sigma}. Then ησ∈C2​(ℝd)\eta_{\sigma}\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and ησ>0\eta_{\sigma}>0. Moreover, ησ\eta_{\sigma} and ∇ησ\nabla\eta_{\sigma} are products of polynomials and Gaussians, so both belong to C0​(ℝd)∩L1​(ℝd)∩L∞​(ℝd)C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). The Hessian ∇2ησ\nabla^{2}\eta_{\sigma} is also a product of a polynomial and a Gaussian, hence belongs to L∞​(ℝd)L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

Finally, for every z∈ℝdz\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

∇ησ​(z)=−zσ2​κσ​(z)=−zc1​κσ​(z),\nabla\eta_{\sigma}(z)=-\frac{z}{\sigma^{2}}\kappa_{\sigma}(z)=-\frac{z}{c_{1}}\kappa_{\sigma}(z),

and with λ1=0\lambda_{1}=0, λ0=c2=1\lambda_{0}=c_{2}=1,

(λ0​I−λ1​Δ)​ησ​(z)=ησ​(z)=κσ​(z)=c2​κσ​(z).(\lambda_{0}I-\lambda_{1}\Delta)\eta_{\sigma}(z)=\eta_{\sigma}(z)=\kappa_{\sigma}(z)=c_{2}\kappa_{\sigma}(z).

Thus all conditions of Assumption 5.2 hold. ∎

Lemma 5.8 (W1,∞W^{1,\infty} regularity from a bounded radial derivative).

Let ϕ∈C⁡([0,∞))∩C1​((0,∞))\phi\in C([0,\infty))\cap C^{1}((0,\infty)) be bounded and satisfy

M:=supr>0|ϕ′​(r)|<∞.M:=\sup_{r>0}\left\lvert\phi^{\prime}(r)\right\rvert<\infty.

Define f:ℝd→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} by

f⁡(x):=ϕ⁡(‖x‖).f(x):=\phi(\left\lVert x\right\rVert).

Then f∈W1,∞​(ℝd)f\in W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Moreover, ff is globally Lipschitz, Lip⁡(f)≤M\operatorname{Lip}(f)\leq M, and for almost every x≠0x\neq 0,

∇f​(x)=ϕ′​(‖x‖)​x‖x‖.\nabla f(x)=\phi^{\prime}(\left\lVert x\right\rVert)\frac{x}{\left\lVert x\right\rVert}.

Consequently,

‖∇f‖L∞​(ℝd)≤M.\left\lVert\nabla f\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\leq M.
Proof.

First, we show that ϕ\phi is MM-Lipschitz on [0,∞)[0,\infty). If r>s>0r>s>0, then the mean value theorem gives

|ϕ⁡(r)−ϕ⁡(s)|≤M​|r−s|.\left\lvert\phi(r)-\phi(s)\right\rvert\leq M\left\lvert r-s\right\rvert.

For r>0r>0 and ε∈(0,r)\varepsilon\in(0,r),

|ϕ⁡(r)−ϕ⁡(ε)|≤M⁡(r−ε),\left\lvert\phi(r)-\phi(\varepsilon)\right\rvert\leq M(r-\varepsilon),

and letting ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0 while using the continuity of ϕ\phi at 00 gives

|ϕ⁡(r)−ϕ⁡(0)|≤M​r.\left\lvert\phi(r)-\phi(0)\right\rvert\leq Mr.

Therefore, for all r,s≥0r,s\geq 0,

|ϕ⁡(r)−ϕ⁡(s)|≤M​|r−s|.\left\lvert\phi(r)-\phi(s)\right\rvert\leq M\left\lvert r-s\right\rvert.

Consequently, for arbitrary x,y∈ℝdx,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

|f⁡(x)−f⁡(y)|≤M​|‖x‖−‖y‖|≤M⁡‖x−y‖,\left\lvert f(x)-f(y)\right\rvert\leq M\left\lvert\left\lVert x\right\rVert-\left\lVert y\right\rVert\right\rvert\leq M\left\lVert x-y\right\rVert,

so ff is globally Lipschitz. Since ϕ\phi is bounded, f∈L∞​(ℝd)f\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

By Rademacher’s theorem [5], ff is differentiable almost everywhere. At such differentiability points with x≠0x\neq 0, the map z↦‖z‖z\mapsto\left\lVert z\right\rVert is C1C^{1} on ℝd∖{0}\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus\{0\}, and the chain rule gives

∇f​(x)=ϕ′​(‖x‖)​x‖x‖.\nabla f(x)=\phi^{\prime}(\left\lVert x\right\rVert)\frac{x}{\left\lVert x\right\rVert}.

Hence, almost everywhere,

‖∇f​(x)‖≤M.\left\lVert\nabla f(x)\right\rVert\leq M. (5.13)

A Lipschitz function belongs to Wloc1,∞​(ℝd)W^{1,\infty}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), and its weak derivative agrees almost everywhere with its classical gradient [5]. Combining the L∞L^{\infty} bound in (5.13) with f∈L∞​(ℝd)f\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) yields f∈W1,∞​(ℝd)f\in W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). ∎

Proposition 5.9 (The Matérn kernel satisfies the companion-elliptic hypothesis).

Fix ℓ>0\ell>0 and ν≥12\nu\geq\tfrac{1}{2}. Let KνK_{\nu} be the modified Bessel function of the second kind, and define

κν,ℓ​(z):=ℓ​‖z‖ν​Kν​(‖z‖ℓ),ην,ℓ​(z):=‖z‖ν+1​Kν+1​(‖z‖ℓ).\kappa_{\nu,\ell}(z):=\ell\,\left\lVert z\right\rVert^{\nu}K_{\nu}\!\left(\frac{\left\lVert z\right\rVert}{\ell}\right),\qquad\eta_{\nu,\ell}(z):=\left\lVert z\right\rVert^{\nu+1}K_{\nu+1}\!\left(\frac{\left\lVert z\right\rVert}{\ell}\right). (5.14)

The values at z=0z=0 are defined by continuous extension; see [8, 18, 19]. Then Assumption 5.2 holds.

Proof.

For r>0r>0, set the radial profiles

ϕ⁡(r):=ℓ​rν​Kν​(r/ℓ),ψ⁡(r):=rν+1​Kν+1​(r/ℓ).\phi(r):=\ell\,r^{\nu}K_{\nu}(r/\ell),\qquad\psi(r):=r^{\nu+1}K_{\nu+1}(r/\ell).

Then, for z≠0z\neq 0, κν,ℓ​(z)=ϕ⁡(‖z‖)\kappa_{\nu,\ell}(z)=\phi(\left\lVert z\right\rVert) and ην,ℓ​(z)=ψ⁡(‖z‖)\eta_{\nu,\ell}(z)=\psi(\left\lVert z\right\rVert). We use the identities [11]

dd​s​(sμ​Kμ​(s))=−sμ​Kμ−1​(s),\frac{d}{ds}\bigl(s^{\mu}K_{\mu}(s)\bigr)=-s^{\mu}K_{\mu-1}(s), (5.15)
Kμ+1​(s)=Kμ−1​(s)+2​μs​Kμ​(s).K_{\mu+1}(s)=K_{\mu-1}(s)+\frac{2\mu}{s}K_{\mu}(s). (5.16)

These identities imply, for r>0r>0,

ψ′​(r)=dd​r​(rν+1​Kν+1​(r/ℓ))=−rℓ2​ϕ​(r),\psi^{\prime}(r)=\frac{d}{dr}\Bigl(r^{\nu+1}K_{\nu+1}(r/\ell)\Bigr)=-\frac{r}{\ell^{2}}\,\phi(r), (5.17)

and

ϕ′​(r)=−rν​Kν−1​(r/ℓ).\phi^{\prime}(r)=-r^{\nu}K_{\nu-1}(r/\ell). (5.18)

Moreover, (5.16) and (5.18) yield

We first prove the companion-elliptic identities on ℝd∖{0}\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus\{0\}. For z≠0z\neq 0 and r=‖z‖r=\left\lVert z\right\rVert, the radial gradient formula gives

∇ην,ℓ​(z)=ψ′​(r)​zr=−zℓ2​ϕ​(r)=−zℓ2​κν,ℓ​(z),\nabla\eta_{\nu,\ell}(z)=\psi^{\prime}(r)\frac{z}{r}=-\frac{z}{\ell^{2}}\,\phi(r)=-\frac{z}{\ell^{2}}\,\kappa_{\nu,\ell}(z), (5.20)

so the first identity in (5.1) holds on ℝd∖{0}\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus\{0\}. Also, by the radial Laplacian formula and (5.17),

Δ​ην,ℓ​(z)=ψ′′​(r)+d−1r​ψ′​(r)=−dℓ2​ϕ​(r)−rℓ2​ϕ′​(r).\Delta\eta_{\nu,\ell}(z)=\psi^{\prime\prime}(r)+\frac{d-1}{r}\psi^{\prime}(r)=-\frac{d}{\ell^{2}}\,\phi(r)-\frac{r}{\ell^{2}}\,\phi^{\prime}(r).

Substituting (5.19), we obtain

(I−ℓ2​Δ)​ην,ℓ​(z)=ψ⁡(r)+d​ϕ​(r)+r​ϕ′​(r)=(d+2​ν)​ϕ​(r)=(d+2​ν)​κν,ℓ​(z).(I-\ell^{2}\Delta)\eta_{\nu,\ell}(z)=\psi(r)+d\,\phi(r)+r\,\phi^{\prime}(r)=(d+2\nu)\phi(r)=(d+2\nu)\kappa_{\nu,\ell}(z). (5.21)

Thus the second identity in (5.1) also holds on ℝd∖{0}\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus\{0\}.

We now check regularity at the origin and decay at infinity. By the small-argument asymptotics [11]

sμKμ(s)⟶2μ−1Γ(μ)(s↓0,μ>0)s^{\mu}K_{\mu}(s)\longrightarrow 2^{\mu-1}\Gamma(\mu)\qquad(s\downarrow 0,\ \mu>0) (5.22)

and

K0​(s)∼−log⁡s(s↓0),K_{0}(s)\sim-\log s\qquad(s\downarrow 0), (5.23)

as well as

Kμ​(s)=π2​s​e−s​(1+O⁡(s−1))(s→∞),K_{\mu}(s)=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2s}}e^{-s}\bigl(1+O(s^{-1})\bigr)\qquad(s\to\infty), (5.24)

the functions ϕ\phi and ψ\psi have finite positive limits at r=0r=0. We define ϕ⁡(0)\phi(0) and ψ⁡(0)\psi(0) by these limits, thereby defining the continuous extensions of κν,ℓ\kappa_{\nu,\ell} and ην,ℓ\eta_{\nu,\ell} at the origin. As r→∞r\to\infty, both decay exponentially. Therefore

κν,ℓ,ην,ℓ∈C⁡(ℝd)∩C0​(ℝd)∩L1​(ℝd)∩L∞​(ℝd),κν,ℓ>0,ην,ℓ>0.\kappa_{\nu,\ell},\ \eta_{\nu,\ell}\in C(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\qquad\kappa_{\nu,\ell}>0,\ \eta_{\nu,\ell}>0. (5.25)

From (5.18), (5.22), (5.23), and the symmetry K−ρ=KρK_{-\rho}=K_{\rho} [11], as r↓0r\downarrow 0,

Kν−1​(r/ℓ)={O⁡(r−(1−ν)),12≤ν<1,O⁡(|log⁡r|),ν=1,O⁡(r−(ν−1)),ν>1,K_{\nu-1}(r/\ell)=\begin{cases}O(r^{-(1-\nu)}),&\tfrac{1}{2}\leq\nu<1,\\[3.00003pt] O(\left\lvert\log r\right\rvert),&\nu=1,\\[3.00003pt] O(r^{-(\nu-1)}),&\nu>1,\end{cases}

and hence

ϕ′​(r)={O⁡(r2​ν−1),12≤ν<1,O⁡(r​|log⁡r|),ν=1,O⁡(r),ν>1,(r↓0).\phi^{\prime}(r)=\begin{cases}O(r^{2\nu-1}),&\tfrac{1}{2}\leq\nu<1,\\[3.00003pt] O(r\left\lvert\log r\right\rvert),&\nu=1,\\[3.00003pt] O(r),&\nu>1,\end{cases}\qquad(r\downarrow 0).

Thus ϕ′\phi^{\prime} is bounded near the origin. On the other hand, (5.18) and (5.24) show that ϕ′​(r)\phi^{\prime}(r) decays exponentially as r→∞r\to\infty. Combining this with the continuity of ϕ′\phi^{\prime} on (0,∞)(0,\infty), we obtain

supr>0|ϕ′​(r)|<∞.\sup_{r>0}\left\lvert\phi^{\prime}(r)\right\rvert<\infty. (5.26)

With ϕ​(0):=κν,ℓ​(0)\phi(0):=\kappa_{\nu,\ell}(0), we have ϕ∈C⁡([0,∞))∩C1​((0,∞))∩L∞​(0,∞)\phi\in C([0,\infty))\cap C^{1}((0,\infty))\cap L^{\infty}(0,\infty) and

supr>0|ϕ′​(r)|<∞.\sup_{r>0}\left\lvert\phi^{\prime}(r)\right\rvert<\infty.

Applying Lemma 5.8, we conclude that

κν,ℓ​(z)=ϕ⁡(‖z‖)\kappa_{\nu,\ell}(z)=\phi(\left\lVert z\right\rVert)

belongs to W1,∞​(ℝd)W^{1,\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). In particular, when ν=12\nu=\tfrac{1}{2}, the radial cusp at the origin prevents κν,ℓ\kappa_{\nu,\ell} from being a classical C1C^{1} function, but Assumption 5.2 requires only W1,∞W^{1,\infty} regularity, and the bounded radial derivative estimate in (5.26) provides precisely that regularity.

Next, (5.17) gives, for r>0r>0,

ψ′​(r)r=−1ℓ2​ϕ​(r),ψ′′​(r)=−1ℓ2​ϕ​(r)−rℓ2​ϕ′​(r).\frac{\psi^{\prime}(r)}{r}=-\frac{1}{\ell^{2}}\phi(r),\qquad\psi^{\prime\prime}(r)=-\frac{1}{\ell^{2}}\phi(r)-\frac{r}{\ell^{2}}\phi^{\prime}(r).

Since ϕ∈L∞​(0,∞)\phi\in L^{\infty}(0,\infty),

|ψ′​(r)|≤rℓ2​‖ϕ‖L∞​(0,∞)(r>0).\left\lvert\psi^{\prime}(r)\right\rvert\leq\frac{r}{\ell^{2}}\left\lVert\phi\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}(0,\infty)}\qquad(r>0).

Thus, for any z∈ℝdz\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with r=‖z‖r=\left\lVert z\right\rVert,

|ην,ℓ​(z)−ην,ℓ​(0)|=|ψ⁡(r)−ψ⁡(0)|≤∫0r|ψ′​(t)|​𝑑t≤‖ϕ‖L∞​(0,∞)2​ℓ2​r2.\left\lvert\eta_{\nu,\ell}(z)-\eta_{\nu,\ell}(0)\right\rvert=\left\lvert\psi(r)-\psi(0)\right\rvert\leq\int_{0}^{r}\left\lvert\psi^{\prime}(t)\right\rvert\,dt\leq\frac{\left\lVert\phi\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}(0,\infty)}}{2\ell^{2}}r^{2}. (5.27)

Therefore ην,ℓ\eta_{\nu,\ell} is differentiable at the origin and ∇ην,ℓ​(0)=0\nabla\eta_{\nu,\ell}(0)=0. For z≠0z\neq 0 we already know that

∇ην,ℓ​(z)=ψ′​(‖z‖)​z‖z‖.\nabla\eta_{\nu,\ell}(z)=\psi^{\prime}(\left\lVert z\right\rVert)\frac{z}{\left\lVert z\right\rVert}.

Combining this with (5.27) and (5.24), we obtain ∇ην,ℓ∈C0​(ℝd,ℝd)∩L∞​(ℝd,ℝd)\nabla\eta_{\nu,\ell}\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{R}^{d})\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{R}^{d}). Also, for z≠0z\neq 0,

|∇ην,ℓ​(z)|=‖z‖ℓ2​κν,ℓ​(z),\left\lvert\nabla\eta_{\nu,\ell}(z)\right\rvert=\frac{\left\lVert z\right\rVert}{\ell^{2}}\,\kappa_{\nu,\ell}(z),

and the right-hand side is O⁡(‖z‖)O(\left\lVert z\right\rVert) near the origin and decays exponentially at infinity. Hence ∇ην,ℓ∈L1​(ℝd,ℝd)\nabla\eta_{\nu,\ell}\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{R}^{d}).

We now consider the Hessian. From (5.17), the identity ψ′′​(r)=−ℓ−2​ϕ​(r)−ℓ−2​r​ϕ′​(r)\psi^{\prime\prime}(r)=-\ell^{-2}\phi(r)-\ell^{-2}r\phi^{\prime}(r), and the limits ϕ⁡(r)→ϕ⁡(0)\phi(r)\to\phi(0) and r​ϕ′​(r)→0r\phi^{\prime}(r)\to 0 as r↓0r\downarrow 0, we obtain

ψ′​(r)r→−ϕ⁡(0)ℓ2,ψ′′(r)→−ϕ⁡(0)ℓ2(r↓0).\frac{\psi^{\prime}(r)}{r}\to-\frac{\phi(0)}{\ell^{2}},\qquad\psi^{\prime\prime}(r)\to-\frac{\phi(0)}{\ell^{2}}\qquad(r\downarrow 0). (5.28)

∂i​jην,ℓ​(z)=ψ′′​(r)​zi​zjr2+ψ′​(r)r​(δi​j−zi​zjr2)\partial_{ij}\eta_{\nu,\ell}(z)=\psi^{\prime\prime}(r)\frac{z_{i}z_{j}}{r^{2}}+\frac{\psi^{\prime}(r)}{r}\left(\delta_{ij}-\frac{z_{i}z_{j}}{r^{2}}\right)

∂i​jην,ℓ​(z)→−ϕ⁡(0)ℓ2​δi​j(z→0).\partial_{ij}\eta_{\nu,\ell}(z)\to-\frac{\phi(0)}{\ell^{2}}\delta_{ij}\qquad(z\to 0). (5.29)

On the other hand, if eje_{j} denotes the jj-th standard basis vector, then for t≠0t\neq 0,

∂iην,ℓ​(t​ej)−∂iην,ℓ​(0)t=−δi​jℓ2​κν,ℓ​(t​ej)→−κν,ℓ​(0)ℓ2​δi​j(t→0),\frac{\partial_{i}\eta_{\nu,\ell}(te_{j})-\partial_{i}\eta_{\nu,\ell}(0)}{t}=-\frac{\delta_{ij}}{\ell^{2}}\,\kappa_{\nu,\ell}(te_{j})\to-\frac{\kappa_{\nu,\ell}(0)}{\ell^{2}}\delta_{ij}\qquad(t\to 0),

∂i​jην,ℓ​(0)=−κν,ℓ​(0)ℓ2​δi​j.\partial_{ij}\eta_{\nu,\ell}(0)=-\frac{\kappa_{\nu,\ell}(0)}{\ell^{2}}\delta_{ij}.

D2​ην,ℓ​(0)=−κν,ℓ​(0)ℓ2​Id,∇2ην,ℓ∈L∞​(ℝd).D^{2}\eta_{\nu,\ell}(0)=-\frac{\kappa_{\nu,\ell}(0)}{\ell^{2}}I_{d},\qquad\nabla^{2}\eta_{\nu,\ell}\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

It remains to extend the punctured-space identities (5.20) and (5.21) to all of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. The functions ∇ην,ℓ\nabla\eta_{\nu,\ell} and z↦−(z/ℓ2)​κν,ℓ​(z)z\mapsto-(z/\ell^{2})\kappa_{\nu,\ell}(z) are continuous on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and agree on ℝd∖{0}\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus\{0\}, and hence

∇ην,ℓ​(z)=−zℓ2​κν,ℓ​(z)(z∈ℝd).\nabla\eta_{\nu,\ell}(z)=-\frac{z}{\ell^{2}}\,\kappa_{\nu,\ell}(z)\qquad(z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}).

(I−ℓ2​Δ)​ην,ℓ​(z)=(d+2​ν)​κν,ℓ​(z)(z∈ℝd).(I-\ell^{2}\Delta)\eta_{\nu,\ell}(z)=(d+2\nu)\kappa_{\nu,\ell}(z)\qquad(z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}).

Therefore both the regularity requirements and the companion identities in Assumption 5.2 hold. ∎

Moreover, the spectral non-vanishing property used in the last step of the field-identifiability proof can also be verified separately. Let β:=ν+d/2\beta:=\nu+d/2. Then β>d/2\beta>d/2, and by Lemma 3.3,

ℱ−1​((1+ℓ2​‖⋅‖2)−β)\mathcal{F}^{-1}\Bigl(\bigl(1+\ell^{2}\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert^{2}\bigr)^{-\beta}\Bigr)

agrees on ℝd∖{0}\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus\{0\} with a positive constant multiple of κν,ℓ\kappa_{\nu,\ell}. Since (5.25) gives κν,ℓ∈L1​(ℝd)\kappa_{\nu,\ell}\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), taking the Fourier transform yields a constant Cd,ν,ℓ>0C_{d,\nu,\ell}>0 such that

κ^ν,ℓ​(ξ)=Cd,ν,ℓ​(1+ℓ2​‖ξ‖2)−(ν+d/2),Cd,ν,ℓ>0.\widehat{\kappa}_{\nu,\ell}(\xi)=C_{d,\nu,\ell}\bigl(1+\ell^{2}\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert^{2}\bigr)^{-(\nu+d/2)},\qquad C_{d,\nu,\ell}>0.

In particular, this is strictly positive for every ξ∈ℝd\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Theorem 5.10 (Classification of the companion-elliptic mechanism).

Assume Assumption 5.2. Then, up to a positive scalar multiple, every companion-elliptic kernel is either a Gaussian kernel or a Matérn kernel with ν≥12\nu\geq\tfrac{1}{2}. More precisely:

  1. (i)

    if λ1=0\lambda_{1}=0, then κ\kappa is a positive scalar multiple of a Gaussian kernel;

  2. (ii)

    if λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0, then κ\kappa is a positive scalar multiple of a Matérn kernel κν,ℓ\kappa_{\nu,\ell} for some ν≥12\nu\geq\tfrac{1}{2} and ℓ>0\ell>0.

In particular, every companion-elliptic kernel κ\kappa is radial.

Proof.

If λ1=0\lambda_{1}=0, then Lemma 5.5 gives

κ^​(ξ)=κ^​(0)​exp⁡(−c1​c22​λ0​‖ξ‖2).\widehat{\kappa}(\xi)=\widehat{\kappa}(0)\exp\!\left(-\frac{c_{1}c_{2}}{2\lambda_{0}}\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert^{2}\right).

The inverse Fourier transform of a Gaussian is again a Gaussian, so κ\kappa is a positive scalar multiple of a Gaussian kernel.

Now assume λ1>0\lambda_{1}>0. Set

ℓ2:=λ1λ0,β:=c1​c22​λ1.\ell^{2}:=\frac{\lambda_{1}}{\lambda_{0}},\qquad\beta:=\frac{c_{1}c_{2}}{2\lambda_{1}}. (5.30)

Then, by Lemma 5.5,

κ^​(ξ)=κ^​(0)​(1+ℓ2​‖ξ‖2)−β.\widehat{\kappa}(\xi)=\widehat{\kappa}(0)\bigl(1+\ell^{2}\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert^{2}\bigr)^{-\beta}. (5.31)

Let ν:=β−d/2\nu:=\beta-d/2. We now apply Gaussian regularization to the frequency-domain representation (5.31) to derive the spatial form of κ\kappa. For ε>0\varepsilon>0, set

mε​(ξ):=e−ε​‖ξ‖2​(1+ℓ2​‖ξ‖2)−β(ξ∈ℝd).m_{\varepsilon}(\xi):=e^{-\varepsilon\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert^{2}}\bigl(1+\ell^{2}\left\lVert\xi\right\rVert^{2}\bigr)^{-\beta}\qquad(\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{d}). (5.32)

Then mε∈L1​(ℝd)m_{\varepsilon}\in L^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Using the gamma identity [11], Lemma 3.1, and Tonelli’s theorem, we obtain, for all x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

ℱ−1​mε​(x)\displaystyle\mathcal{F}^{-1}m_{\varepsilon}(x) =1Γ⁡(β)​∫0∞tβ−1​e−t​ℱ−1​(e−(ε+t​ℓ2)​‖⋅‖2)​(x)​𝑑t\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\beta)}\int_{0}^{\infty}t^{\beta-1}e^{-t}\mathcal{F}^{-1}\bigl(e^{-(\varepsilon+t\ell^{2})\left\lVert\cdot\right\rVert^{2}}\bigr)(x)\,dt
=πd/2Γ⁡(β)∫0∞tβ−1e−t(ε+tℓ2)−d/2exp(−‖x‖24​(ε+t​ℓ2))dt.\displaystyle=\frac{\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(\beta)}\int_{0}^{\infty}t^{\beta-1}e^{-t}(\varepsilon+t\ell^{2})^{-d/2}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\left\lVert x\right\rVert^{2}}{4(\varepsilon+t\ell^{2})}\right)dt.

Fix x≠0x\neq 0. The function s↦s−d/2e−‖x‖2/(4s)s\mapsto s^{-d/2}e^{-\left\lVert x\right\rVert^{2}/(4s)} is bounded on (0,∞)(0,\infty), so for 0<t≤10<t\leq 1 the integrand above is dominated by C​tβ−1Ct^{\beta-1}. For t≥1t\geq 1, we have (ε+tℓ2)−d/2≤(ℓ2t)−d/2(\varepsilon+t\ell^{2})^{-d/2}\leq(\ell^{2}t)^{-d/2} and the exponential factor is at most 11, so the integrand is dominated by C​tβ−1−d/2​e−tCt^{\beta-1-d/2}e^{-t}. Therefore, by dominated convergence,

ℱ−1​mε​(x)⟶πd/2Γ⁡(β)​ℓd​∫0∞tβ−d/2−1​e−t−‖x‖2/(4​ℓ2​t)​𝑑t(ε↓0).\mathcal{F}^{-1}m_{\varepsilon}(x)\longrightarrow\frac{\pi^{d/2}}{\Gamma(\beta)\ell^{d}}\int_{0}^{\infty}t^{\beta-d/2-1}e^{-t-\left\lVert x\right\rVert^{2}/(4\ell^{2}t)}\,dt\qquad(\varepsilon\downarrow 0). (5.33)

Using the integral representation of the modified Bessel function [11] (in the form valid for r>0r>0 and all real ν\nu, with negative ν\nu interpreted through the identity K−ν=KνK_{-\nu}=K_{\nu}), the right-hand side of (5.33) equals

C~d,β,ℓ​‖x‖ν​Kν​(‖x‖ℓ)\widetilde{C}_{d,\beta,\ell}\,\left\lVert x\right\rVert^{\nu}K_{\nu}\!\left(\frac{\left\lVert x\right\rVert}{\ell}\right) (5.34)

for some positive constant C~d,β,ℓ>0\widetilde{C}_{d,\beta,\ell}>0.

Now set

6 Field stability in the companion-elliptic class

Theorem 5.6 resolves the field-identifiability problem. In this section, we address the field-stability problem for the same kernel family. We begin by showing that smallness of the field alone does not guarantee weak convergence on the full class of Borel probability measures, even under locally uniform (compact-open) control or under global L∞L^{\infty} control. Nevertheless, when a sequence of drift fields converges to zero, the only possible limiting defect is a scalar mass defect: every vague cluster point must lie on the one-dimensional ray {c​p:0≤c≤1}\{c\,p:0\leq c\leq 1\}. Therefore, a single additional scalar observable suffices to restore weak convergence.

6.1 Why smallness of the field alone does not guarantee stability

The first counterexample has a particularly simple form: most of the mass remains distributed according to pp, while a fixed amount of satellite mass is sent to infinity.

Lemma 6.1.

Assume Assumption 5.2. Then

κ∈C0​(ℝd),z⟼z​κ​(z)∈C0​(ℝd,ℝd).\kappa\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\qquad z\longmapsto z\,\kappa(z)\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d};\mathbb{R}^{d}).

fx​(y):=κ⁡(x−y),gx,j​(y):=yj​κ​(x−y)f_{x}(y):=\kappa(x-y),\qquad g_{x,j}(y):=y_{j}\,\kappa(x-y)

κ∈C0​(ℝd).\kappa\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

For fixed xx and jj,

gx,j​(y)=xj​κ​(x−y)−(xj−yj)​κ​(x−y),g_{x,j}(y)=x_{j}\kappa(x-y)-(x_{j}-y_{j})\kappa(x-y),

which is a sum of translates of the C0C_{0} functions z↦κ⁡(z)z\mapsto\kappa(z) and z↦zj​κ​(z)z\mapsto z_{j}\kappa(z). Thus both fxf_{x} and gx,jg_{x,j} belong to C0​(ℝd)C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). ∎

The next counterexample shows that even global uniform control of the field is insufficient.

Counterexample 6.3.

Assume Assumption 5.2. Then there exist a Borel probability measure pp and a sequence of probability measures qnq_{n} such that

Counterexamples 6.2 and 6.3 show that smallness of the field alone does not guarantee weak convergence on the full class of Borel probability measures.

6.2 Vague cluster points and the defect ray

Despite the counterexamples in Counterexamples 6.2 and 6.3, convergence of the field to zero imposes strong structural constraints on the asymptotic behavior of probability measures. In this subsection, we identify these constraints. For the compactness argument, we use vague convergence against C0​(ℝd)C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) test functions.

Definition 6.4 (C0C_{0}-vague convergence).

For finite Borel measures μn,μ\mu_{n},\mu on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, we write

μn→𝑣μ\mu_{n}\xrightarrow{v}\mu

and say that μn\mu_{n} converges C0C_{0}-vaguely to μ\mu if, for every f∈C0​(ℝd)f\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),

∫ℝdf​d​μn→∫ℝdf​𝑑μ.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}f\,d\mu_{n}\to\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}f\,d\mu.

In this paper, we refer to this C0C_{0}-based convergence simply as vague convergence. It should be distinguished from the classical vague topology based on Cc​(ℝd)C_{c}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), which is frequently used in the literature.

We also denote by

ℳ≤1​(ℝd)\mathcal{M}_{\leq 1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})

the set of finite nonnegative Borel measures with total mass at most 11.

Lemma 6.5 (Vague compactness for probability measures).

Every sequence (qn)⊂𝒫⁡(ℝd)(q_{n})\subset\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) of probability measures has a subsequence that converges vaguely to some μ∈ℳ≤1​(ℝd)\mu\in\mathcal{M}_{\leq 1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

Proof.

Let ℝd¯:=ℝd∪{∞}\overline{\mathbb{R}^{d}}:=\mathbb{R}^{d}\cup\{\infty\} be the one-point compactification. Each qnq_{n} is a Borel probability measure on the compact metrizable space ℝd¯\overline{\mathbb{R}^{d}}. By compactness of the weak topology on 𝒫⁡(ℝd¯)\mathcal{P}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^{d}}) [4, 7], there exist a subsequence (qnk)(q_{n_{k}}) and a probability measure μ¯\bar{\mu} on ℝd¯\overline{\mathbb{R}^{d}} such that

qnk⇒μ¯in ​𝒫​(ℝd¯).q_{n_{k}}\Rightarrow\bar{\mu}\qquad\text{in }\mathcal{P}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^{d}}).

Let μ\mu be the restriction of μ¯\bar{\mu} to ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Then μ∈ℳ≤1​(ℝd)\mu\in\mathcal{M}_{\leq 1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

Now fix f∈C0​(ℝd)f\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Extend ff to ℝd¯\overline{\mathbb{R}^{d}} by setting f⁡(∞)=0f(\infty)=0. Since f⁡(x)→0f(x)\to 0 as ‖x‖→∞\left\lVert x\right\rVert\to\infty, this extension is continuous. Therefore

∫ℝdf​d​qnk=∫ℝd¯f​d​qnk→∫ℝd¯f​𝑑μ¯=∫ℝdf​𝑑μ.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}f\,dq_{n_{k}}=\int_{\overline{\mathbb{R}^{d}}}f\,dq_{n_{k}}\to\int_{\overline{\mathbb{R}^{d}}}f\,d\bar{\mu}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}f\,d\mu.

Thus qnk→𝑣μq_{n_{k}}\xrightarrow{v}\mu. ∎

Remark 6.6 (A metrizable realization of the vague topology).

Define

ι:ℳ≤1​(ℝd)→𝒫⁡(ℝd¯),ι⁡(μ):=μ+(1−μ⁡(ℝd))​δ∞.\iota:\mathcal{M}_{\leq 1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\to\mathcal{P}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^{d}}),\qquad\iota(\mu):=\mu+\bigl(1-\mu(\mathbb{R}^{d})\bigr)\delta_{\infty}.

Then μn→𝑣μ\mu_{n}\xrightarrow{v}\mu is equivalent to ι⁡(μn)⇒ι⁡(μ)\iota(\mu_{n})\Rightarrow\iota(\mu). Therefore the C0C_{0}-vague topology on ℳ≤1​(ℝd)\mathcal{M}_{\leq 1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), which we call the vague topology in this paper, is obtained by pulling back the weak topology on the compact metrizable space 𝒫⁡(ℝd¯)\mathcal{P}(\overline{\mathbb{R}^{d}}) [4, 7]. The subsequence arguments below are justified by this realization.

Lemma 6.7 (Vague convergence to a probability measure implies tightness and weak convergence).

Let (qn)⊂𝒫⁡(ℝd)(q_{n})\subset\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and p∈𝒫⁡(ℝd)p\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) satisfy

qn→𝑣p.q_{n}\xrightarrow{v}p.

Then (qn)(q_{n}) is tight and

qn⇒p.q_{n}\Rightarrow p.
Proof.

Fix δ>0\delta>0. By inner regularity of the probability measure pp [4, 6], there exists a compact set Kδp⊂ℝdK_{\delta}^{p}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} such that

p⁡(Kδp)>1−δ.p(K_{\delta}^{p})>1-\delta.

Choose an open ball BR​(0)B_{R}(0) containing KδpK_{\delta}^{p}. Then Kδp⊂BR​(0)K_{\delta}^{p}\subset B_{R}(0) and BR​(0)¯\overline{B_{R}(0)} is compact. By Urysohn’s lemma on the locally compact Hausdorff space ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} [6], there exists χδ∈Cc​(ℝd)\chi_{\delta}\in C_{c}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) such that

0≤χδ≤1,χδ≡1​ on ​Kδp,supp⁡χδ⊂BR​(0).0\leq\chi_{\delta}\leq 1,\qquad\chi_{\delta}\equiv 1\text{ on }K_{\delta}^{p},\qquad\supp\chi_{\delta}\subset B_{R}(0).

In particular,

∫χδ​𝑑p≥p⁡(Kδp)>1−δ.\int\chi_{\delta}\,dp\geq p(K_{\delta}^{p})>1-\delta.

By vague convergence, there exists Nδ∈ℕN_{\delta}\in\mathbb{N} such that, for all n≥Nδn\geq N_{\delta},

∫χδ​d​qn>1−δ.\int\chi_{\delta}\,dq_{n}>1-\delta.

Thus

qn​(supp⁡χδ)≥∫χδ​d​qn>1−δ(n≥Nδ).q_{n}(\supp\chi_{\delta})\geq\int\chi_{\delta}\,dq_{n}>1-\delta\qquad(n\geq N_{\delta}).

For each 1≤n<Nδ1\leq n<N_{\delta}, use inner regularity of qnq_{n} to choose a compact set Kδ,n⊂ℝdK_{\delta,n}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} such that

qn​(Kδ,n)>1−δ.q_{n}(K_{\delta,n})>1-\delta.

Then

Kδ:=supp⁡χδ∪⋃n=1Nδ−1Kδ,nK_{\delta}:=\supp\chi_{\delta}\cup\bigcup_{n=1}^{N_{\delta}-1}K_{\delta,n}

is compact and satisfies

p⁡(Kδ)≥p⁡(Kδp)>1−δ,qn​(Kδ)>1−δfor every ​n∈ℕ.p(K_{\delta})\geq p(K_{\delta}^{p})>1-\delta,\qquad q_{n}(K_{\delta})>1-\delta\quad\text{for every }n\in\mathbb{N}. (6.2)

Thus (qn)(q_{n}) is tight.

Now let f∈Cb​(ℝd)f\in C_{b}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) be arbitrary and fix ε>0\varepsilon>0. Apply the tightness established in (6.2) with δ=ε\delta=\varepsilon to choose a compact set KεK_{\varepsilon} such that

p(Kε)>1−ε,qn(Kε)>1−εfor every n.p(K_{\varepsilon})>1-\varepsilon,\qquad q_{n}(K_{\varepsilon})>1-\varepsilon\quad\text{for every }n.

By Urysohn’s lemma again, choose χε∈Cc​(ℝd)\chi_{\varepsilon}\in C_{c}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) such that

0≤χε≤1,χε≡1​ on ​Kε.0\leq\chi_{\varepsilon}\leq 1,\qquad\chi_{\varepsilon}\equiv 1\text{ on }K_{\varepsilon}.

Then f​χε∈C0​(ℝd)f\chi_{\varepsilon}\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), so vague convergence gives

∫f​χε​d​qn→∫f​χε​𝑑p.\int f\chi_{\varepsilon}\,dq_{n}\to\int f\chi_{\varepsilon}\,dp.

Since 0≤1−χε≤𝟏Kεc0\leq 1-\chi_{\varepsilon}\leq\mathbf{1}_{K_{\varepsilon}^{c}},

|∫f​d​qn−∫f​χε​d​qn|≤‖f‖L∞​qn​(Kεc)≤ε​‖f‖L∞,\left\lvert\int f\,dq_{n}-\int f\chi_{\varepsilon}\,dq_{n}\right\rvert\leq\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}}q_{n}(K_{\varepsilon}^{c})\leq\varepsilon\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}},

and similarly

|∫f​𝑑p−∫f​χε​𝑑p|≤ε​‖f‖L∞.\left\lvert\int f\,dp-\int f\chi_{\varepsilon}\,dp\right\rvert\leq\varepsilon\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}}.

Therefore

lim supn→∞|∫f​d​qn−∫f​𝑑p|≤2​ε​‖f‖L∞.\limsup_{n\to\infty}\left\lvert\int f\,dq_{n}-\int f\,dp\right\rvert\leq 2\varepsilon\left\lVert f\right\rVert_{L^{\infty}}.

Since ε>0\varepsilon>0 was arbitrary,

∫f​d​qn→∫f​𝑑pfor every ​f∈Cb​(ℝd).\int f\,dq_{n}\to\int f\,dp\qquad\text{for every }f\in C_{b}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

Hence qn⇒pq_{n}\Rightarrow p. ∎

Proposition 6.8 (All vague cluster points lie on the defect ray).

Assume Assumption 5.2, and fix p∈𝒫⁡(ℝd)p\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Let (qn)⊂𝒫⁡(ℝd)(q_{n})\subset\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) satisfy

Vp,qnκ​(x)→0for every ​x∈ℝd.V_{p,q_{n}}^{\kappa}(x)\to 0\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

If some subsequence converges vaguely as

qnk→𝑣μfor some ​μ∈ℳ≤1​(ℝd),q_{n_{k}}\xrightarrow{v}\mu\qquad\text{for some }\mu\in\mathcal{M}_{\leq 1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),

then

μ=c​pfor some ​c∈[0,1].\mu=c\,p\qquad\text{for some }c\in[0,1].
Proof.

If μ=0\mu=0, the conclusion holds by taking c=0c=0. Now assume μ≠0\mu\neq 0 and set

c:=μ⁡(ℝd)∈(0,1],μ¯:=μ/c∈𝒫⁡(ℝd).c:=\mu(\mathbb{R}^{d})\in(0,1],\qquad\bar{\mu}:=\mu/c\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d}).

Fix x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and j∈{1,…,d}j\in\{1,\dots,d\}. By Lemma 6.1,

fx​(y):=κ⁡(x−y),gx,j​(y):=yj​κ​(x−y)f_{x}(y):=\kappa(x-y),\qquad g_{x,j}(y):=y_{j}\,\kappa(x-y)

belong to C0​(ℝd)C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Hence vague convergence gives

uqnkκ​(x)=∫fx​d​qnk→∫fx​𝑑μ=c​uμ¯κ​(x),u_{q_{n_{k}}}^{\kappa}(x)=\int f_{x}\,dq_{n_{k}}\to\int f_{x}\,d\mu=c\,u_{\bar{\mu}}^{\kappa}(x),
mqnk,jκ​(x)=∫gx,j​d​qnk→∫gx,j​𝑑μ=c​mμ¯,jκ​(x).m_{q_{n_{k}},j}^{\kappa}(x)=\int g_{x,j}\,dq_{n_{k}}\to\int g_{x,j}\,d\mu=c\,m_{\bar{\mu},j}^{\kappa}(x).

Since κ>0\kappa>0 and μ¯∈𝒫⁡(ℝd)\bar{\mu}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), one has uμ¯κ​(x)>0u_{\bar{\mu}}^{\kappa}(x)>0 for every xx. Therefore

aqnkκ​(x)→aμ¯κ​(x).a_{q_{n_{k}}}^{\kappa}(x)\to a_{\bar{\mu}}^{\kappa}(x).

On the other hand, by assumption,

aqnkκ​(x)=apκ​(x)−Vp,qnkκ​(x)→apκ​(x),a_{q_{n_{k}}}^{\kappa}(x)=a_{p}^{\kappa}(x)-V_{p,q_{n_{k}}}^{\kappa}(x)\to a_{p}^{\kappa}(x),

so, for every x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

aμ¯κ​(x)=apκ​(x).a_{\bar{\mu}}^{\kappa}(x)=a_{p}^{\kappa}(x).

Equivalently,

Vp,μ¯κ≡0.V_{p,\bar{\mu}}^{\kappa}\equiv 0.

By the field identifiability of Theorem 5.6,

μ¯=p.\bar{\mu}=p.

Thus μ=c​p\mu=c\,p. ∎

This proposition shows that, when the field converges to zero, asymptotic limits have only one degree of freedom: the scalar mass defect cc that parametrizes the ray. The next theorem shows that, once one adds a scalar observable that is continuous under vague convergence and fixes this single parameter, full weak convergence is restored.

6.3 Generic scale-fixing principle

Theorem 6.9 (Generic scale-fixing principle).

Assume Assumption 5.2, and fix p∈𝒫⁡(ℝd)p\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Let

F:ℳ≤1​(ℝd)→ℝF:\mathcal{M}_{\leq 1}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\to\mathbb{R}

be sequentially continuous with respect to vague convergence. Assume also that the following strict scale-separation condition holds for every c∈[0,1)c\in[0,1):

F⁡(c​p)<F⁡(p).F(c\,p)<F(p). (6.3)

If a sequence of probability measures (qn)⊂𝒫⁡(ℝd)(q_{n})\subset\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) satisfies

Vp,qnκ​(x)→0for every ​x∈ℝd,V_{p,q_{n}}^{\kappa}(x)\to 0\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

and

lim infn→∞F⁡(qn)≥F⁡(p),\liminf_{n\to\infty}F(q_{n})\geq F(p),

then

qn⇒p.q_{n}\Rightarrow p.
Proof.

Take an arbitrary subsequence (qnℓ)(q_{n_{\ell}}) of (qn)(q_{n}). By Lemma 6.5, we may extract a further subsequence (qnℓm)(q_{n_{\ell_{m}}}) converging vaguely to some measure μ∈ℳ≤1​(ℝd)\mu\in\mathcal{M}_{\leq 1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), i.e.,

qnℓm→𝑣μ.q_{n_{\ell_{m}}}\xrightarrow{v}\mu.

By Proposition 6.8, this limiting measure has the form

μ=c​pfor some ​c∈[0,1].\mu=c\,p\qquad\text{for some }c\in[0,1].

Using the sequential continuity of FF and the definition of the liminf, we obtain

F⁡(μ)=limm→∞F⁡(qnℓm)≥lim infn→∞F⁡(qn)≥F⁡(p).F(\mu)=\lim_{m\to\infty}F(q_{n_{\ell_{m}}})\geq\liminf_{n\to\infty}F(q_{n})\geq F(p). (6.4)

If c<1c<1, then (6.3) gives

F⁡(μ)=F⁡(c​p)<F⁡(p),F(\mu)=F(c\,p)<F(p), (6.5)

contradicting (6.4). Therefore c=1c=1, and hence μ=p\mu=p.

By Remark 6.6, the vague topology on ℳ≤1​(ℝd)\mathcal{M}_{\leq 1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is metrizable. The preceding argument shows that every subsequence of (qn)(q_{n}) has a further subsequence converging vaguely to pp. By the subsequence criterion in metric spaces [7, 4], the original sequence also converges vaguely to pp:

qn→𝑣p.q_{n}\xrightarrow{v}p.

Finally, applying Lemma 6.7 gives the desired weak convergence

qn⇒p.q_{n}\Rightarrow p.

∎

Corollary 6.10 (Sufficiency of a single C0C_{0} observable).

Assume Assumption 5.2, and fix p∈𝒫⁡(ℝd)p\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Suppose that a sequence of probability measures (qn)⊂𝒫⁡(ℝd)(q_{n})\subset\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) satisfies

Vp,qnκ​(x)→0for every ​x∈ℝd.V_{p,q_{n}}^{\kappa}(x)\to 0\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Assume also that there exists f∈C0​(ℝd)f\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) such that

f≥0,∫f​𝑑p>0,lim infn→∞∫f​d​qn≥∫f​𝑑p.f\geq 0,\qquad\int f\,dp>0,\qquad\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f\,dq_{n}\geq\int f\,dp.

Then

qn⇒p.q_{n}\Rightarrow p.
Proof.

Apply Theorem 6.9 to the linear functional

Ff​(μ):=∫f​𝑑μ.F_{f}(\mu):=\int f\,d\mu.

This functional is sequentially continuous with respect to vague convergence on ℳ≤1​(ℝd)\mathcal{M}_{\leq 1}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), and since ∫f​𝑑p>0\int f\,dp>0, for every c∈[0,1)c\in[0,1),

Ff​(c​p)=c​∫f​𝑑p<Ff​(p).F_{f}(c\,p)=c\int f\,dp<F_{f}(p).

Thus all hypotheses of Theorem 6.9 are satisfied, and qn⇒pq_{n}\Rightarrow p follows. ∎

Remark 6.11 (The observable condition and tightness).

A single positive C0C_{0} observable alone does not guarantee tightness of a sequence of measures. For example, for a constant c∈(0,1)c\in(0,1) and a sequence ‖zn‖→∞\left\lVert z_{n}\right\rVert\to\infty, define

qn:=c​δ0+(1−c)​δzn.q_{n}:=c\,\delta_{0}+(1-c)\delta_{z_{n}}.

This sequence is not tight, but for every f∈C0​(ℝd)f\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) one still has

∫f​d​qn→c​f​(0).\int f\,dq_{n}\to c\,f(0).

The key point of Corollary 6.10 is that, once the field converges to zero, the only possible escape mechanism is a scalar defect along the ray c​pc\,p. Therefore a single positive C0C_{0} observable suffices to eliminate this one-dimensional defect and restore weak convergence.

Several natural observables of this kind arise from the drifting framework itself. A canonical linear example is the overlap scalar defined below, which already appears in the normalization used in drifting.

Definition 6.12 (Intrinsic overlap scalar).

For a fixed p∈𝒫⁡(ℝd)p\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and an arbitrary finite Borel measure μ\mu on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, define the intrinsic overlap scalar by

𝒵pκ​(μ):=∫ℝdupκ​(x)​μ​(𝑑x)=∬ℝd×ℝdκ⁡(x−y)​p​(𝑑y)​μ​(𝑑x).\mathcal{Z}_{p}^{\kappa}(\mu):=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}u_{p}^{\kappa}(x)\,\mu(dx)=\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}}\kappa(x-y)\,p(dy)\,\mu(dx).
Remark 6.13 (Representative intrinsic observables).

We continue under the hypotheses of Corollary 6.10; in particular,

Vp,qnκ​(x)→0for every ​x∈ℝd.V_{p,q_{n}}^{\kappa}(x)\to 0\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

A direct application of Corollary 6.10 yields the following three sufficient conditions.

  1. (i)

    If, for some point x∗∈ℝdx_{\ast}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

    uqnκ​(x∗)→upκ​(x∗),u_{q_{n}}^{\kappa}(x_{\ast})\to u_{p}^{\kappa}(x_{\ast}),

    then

    qn⇒p.q_{n}\Rightarrow p.

    This follows by applying Corollary 6.10 to f⁡(y):=κ⁡(x∗−y)f(y):=\kappa(x_{\ast}-y). Here f∈C0​(ℝd)f\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) by Lemma 6.1, and

    ∫f​d​qn=uqnκ​(x∗),∫f​𝑑p=upκ​(x∗)>0.\int f\,dq_{n}=u_{q_{n}}^{\kappa}(x_{\ast}),\qquad\int f\,dp=u_{p}^{\kappa}(x_{\ast})>0.
  2. (ii)

    If, for some point x∗∈ℝdx_{\ast}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

    Ψqnκ​(x∗)→Ψpκ​(x∗),\Psi_{q_{n}}^{\kappa}(x_{\ast})\to\Psi_{p}^{\kappa}(x_{\ast}),

    then

    qn⇒p.q_{n}\Rightarrow p.

    This follows by applying Corollary 6.10 to f⁡(y):=η⁡(x∗−y)∈C0​(ℝd)f(y):=\eta(x_{\ast}-y)\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), for which

    ∫f​d​qn=Ψqnκ​(x∗),∫f​𝑑p=Ψpκ​(x∗)>0.\int f\,dq_{n}=\Psi_{q_{n}}^{\kappa}(x_{\ast}),\qquad\int f\,dp=\Psi_{p}^{\kappa}(x_{\ast})>0.
  3. (iii)

    If the intrinsic overlap scalar satisfies

    lim infn→∞𝒵pκ​(qn)≥𝒵pκ​(p),\liminf_{n\to\infty}\mathcal{Z}_{p}^{\kappa}(q_{n})\geq\mathcal{Z}_{p}^{\kappa}(p),

    then again

    qn⇒p.q_{n}\Rightarrow p.

    By Lemma 5.4, upκ∈C0​(ℝd)u_{p}^{\kappa}\in C_{0}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), so the conclusion follows by applying Corollary 6.10 with f=upκf=u_{p}^{\kappa}. Also, since upκ>0u_{p}^{\kappa}>0,

    𝒵pκ​(p)=∫upκ​𝑑p>0.\mathcal{Z}_{p}^{\kappa}(p)=\int u_{p}^{\kappa}\,dp>0.

7 Conclusion

This paper resolves the identifiability and stability problems for the drifting field underlying the Generative Drifting framework. In particular, within the one-sided raw drifting formulation of Deng et al. [1], we settle the remaining converse problem on the full space of Borel probability measures: for both the Laplace kernel and the companion-elliptic kernel family that contains it, Vp,q≡0V_{p,q}\equiv 0 implies p=qp=q. To prove this, we introduced a new framework, the companion-elliptic kernel class, in which a kernel and its companion function are linked through a second-order elliptic operator. We further showed that this class consists precisely of Gaussian kernels and Matérn kernels with ν≥1/2\nu\geq 1/2.

Concerning the asymptotic stability of drifting fields, we identified an additional limitation: even when the global field norm tends to zero, weak convergence of the underlying probability measures need not follow, because mass may escape to infinity. Nevertheless, we proved that the limiting defect caused by such mass escape is confined to the one-dimensional ray consisting of scalar multiples c⋅pc\cdot p of the target distribution. Building on this observation, we introduced the intrinsic overlap scalar, a scalar observable defined directly by the drifting kernel, and showed that imposing an asymptotic lower bound on this scalar at its target value prevents mass from escaping and restores weak convergence. Taken together, these results provide a rigorous theoretical foundation for the convergence analysis of Generative Drifting models.

β⁡(ρε)→β⁡(ρ)in ​Lloc1.\beta(\rho_{\varepsilon})\to\beta(\rho)\qquad\text{in }L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}.

Also, setting

G⁡(z):=z​β′​(z)−β⁡(z),G(z):=z\beta^{\prime}(z)-\beta(z),

the assumptions imply that GG is continuous and bounded, so dominated convergence on compact sets gives

G⁡(ρε)→G⁡(ρ)in ​Lloc1.G(\rho_{\varepsilon})\to G(\rho)\qquad\text{in }L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}.

Since bb is locally Lipschitz and ∇⋅b=tr⁡(D​b)\nabla\cdot b=\operatorname{tr}(Db) is locally essentially bounded on compact cylinders,

bβ(ρε)→bβ(ρ),G(ρε)∇⋅b→G(ρ)∇⋅bin Lloc1.b\,\beta(\rho_{\varepsilon})\to b\,\beta(\rho),\qquad G(\rho_{\varepsilon})\,\nabla\cdot b\to G(\rho)\,\nabla\cdot b\qquad\text{in }L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}.

Finally, β′\beta^{\prime} is bounded and rε→0r_{\varepsilon}\to 0 in Lloc1L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}, so

β′​(ρε)​rε→0in ​Lloc1.\beta^{\prime}(\rho_{\varepsilon})\,r_{\varepsilon}\to 0\qquad\text{in }L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}.

Passing to the limit in the sense of distributions gives

∂tβ(ρ)+∇⋅(bβ(ρ))+(β′(ρ)ρ−β(ρ))∇⋅b=0.\partial_{t}\beta(\rho)+\nabla\cdot\bigl(b\,\beta(\rho)\bigr)+\bigl(\beta^{\prime}(\rho)\rho-\beta(\rho)\bigr)\nabla\cdot b=0. (A.7)

Finally, to distinguish it from the mollification parameter above, choose a new parameter δ>0\delta>0 and set

βδ​(z):=z2+δ2−δ.\beta_{\delta}(z):=\sqrt{z^{2}+\delta^{2}}-\delta.

Then βδ​(0)=0\beta_{\delta}(0)=0, |βδ′​(z)|≤1|\beta_{\delta}^{\prime}(z)|\leq 1, and

|z​βδ′​(z)−βδ​(z)|=|z2z2+δ2−z2+δ2+δ|≤δ(∀z∈ℝ).\bigl|z\beta_{\delta}^{\prime}(z)-\beta_{\delta}(z)\bigr|=\left|\frac{z^{2}}{\sqrt{z^{2}+\delta^{2}}}-\sqrt{z^{2}+\delta^{2}}+\delta\right|\leq\delta\qquad(\forall z\in\mathbb{R}).

Thus (A.7) applies with β=βδ\beta=\beta_{\delta}. Moreover,

0≤|z|−βδ​(z)≤δ(∀z∈ℝ),0\leq|z|-\beta_{\delta}(z)\leq\delta\qquad(\forall z\in\mathbb{R}),

so βδ​(ρ)→|ρ|\beta_{\delta}(\rho)\to|\rho| in Lloc1L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}. The additional term

(βδ′(ρ)ρ−βδ(ρ))∇⋅b\bigl(\beta^{\prime}_{\delta}(\rho)\rho-\beta_{\delta}(\rho)\bigr)\nabla\cdot b

is dominated on compact sets by δ​|∇⋅b|\delta\,|\nabla\cdot b|, and hence converges to 00 in Lloc1L^{1}_{\mathrm{loc}}. Taking the limit δ↓0\delta\downarrow 0 yields

∂t|ρ|+∇⋅(b​|ρ|)=0\partial_{t}|\rho|+\nabla\cdot(b|\rho|)=0

in the sense of distributions. This proves Theorem 4.2. ∎

Appendix B A global L∞L^{\infty} counterexample for companion-elliptic kernels via slowly varying tilts

This appendix proves Counterexample 6.3. Throughout this appendix, fix a companion-elliptic kernel κ\kappa satisfying Assumption 5.2. The strategy of the proof is to start with a heavy-tailed target distribution pp and apply a slowly varying tilt. On the spatial scale on which the kernel κ\kappa acts, the tilt may be treated as nearly constant, so the normalized local barycenter changes only negligibly. At the global level, however, the amplitude of the tilt sends a fixed amount of mass to infinity.

Proof.

The proof is divided into six steps.

Step 1. By Theorem 5.10, up to a positive scalar multiple, the kernel κ\kappa is either Gaussian or a Matérn kernel κν,ℓ\kappa_{\nu,\ell} for some ν≥12\nu\geq\tfrac{1}{2}. In the Gaussian case, for suitable C,a>0C,a>0,

κ⁡(z)=C​e−a​‖z‖2,\kappa(z)=Ce^{-a\left\lVert z\right\rVert^{2}},

and hence, for every λκ>0\lambda_{\kappa}>0, m≥0m\geq 0, and j∈{0,1,2}j\in\{0,1,2\},

∫ℝd‖z‖j​eλκ​‖z‖​κ​(z)​(1+‖z‖)m​𝑑z<∞.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left\lVert z\right\rVert^{j}e^{\lambda_{\kappa}\left\lVert z\right\rVert}\,\kappa(z)\,(1+\left\lVert z\right\rVert)^{m}\,dz<\infty.

In the Matérn case, the Bessel asymptotic formula (5.24) yields constants Rν,ℓ≥1R_{\nu,\ell}\geq 1 and Cν,ℓ(∞)>0C^{(\infty)}_{\nu,\ell}>0 such that

κ(z)≤Cν,ℓ(∞)(1+‖z‖)ν−1/2e−‖z‖/ℓ(‖z‖≥Rν,ℓ).\kappa(z)\leq C^{(\infty)}_{\nu,\ell}(1+\left\lVert z\right\rVert)^{\nu-1/2}e^{-\left\lVert z\right\rVert/\ell}\qquad(\left\lVert z\right\rVert\geq R_{\nu,\ell}).

Increasing the constant if necessary, we obtain a bound valid for all zz:

κ(z)≤Cν,ℓ(1+‖z‖)ν−1/2e−‖z‖/ℓ(∀z∈ℝd).\kappa(z)\leq C_{\nu,\ell}(1+\left\lVert z\right\rVert)^{\nu-1/2}e^{-\left\lVert z\right\rVert/\ell}\qquad(\forall z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}).

Thus, for any λκ∈(0,1/ℓ)\lambda_{\kappa}\in(0,1/\ell),

‖z‖j​eλκ​‖z‖​κ​(z)​(1+‖z‖)m≤Cj,m,ν,ℓ′​(1+‖z‖)j+m+ν−1/2​e−(1/ℓ−λκ)​‖z‖,\left\lVert z\right\rVert^{j}e^{\lambda_{\kappa}\left\lVert z\right\rVert}\,\kappa(z)\,(1+\left\lVert z\right\rVert)^{m}\leq C^{\prime}_{j,m,\nu,\ell}(1+\left\lVert z\right\rVert)^{j+m+\nu-1/2}e^{-(1/\ell-\lambda_{\kappa})\left\lVert z\right\rVert},

and the right-hand side is integrable. Combining the two cases, we obtain a constant λκ>0\lambda_{\kappa}>0 such that

∫ℝd‖z‖j​eλκ​‖z‖​κ​(z)​(1+‖z‖)m​𝑑z<∞(m≥0,j=0,1,2).\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left\lVert z\right\rVert^{j}e^{\lambda_{\kappa}\left\lVert z\right\rVert}\,\kappa(z)\,(1+\left\lVert z\right\rVert)^{m}\,dz<\infty\qquad(m\geq 0,\ j=0,1,2). (B.1)

Step 2. Fix m>dm>d, and define the probability density on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} by

ρ⁡(y):=Z−1​(1+‖y‖)−m,Z:=∫ℝd(1+‖y‖)−m​𝑑y<∞.\rho(y):=Z^{-1}(1+\left\lVert y\right\rVert)^{-m},\qquad Z:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}(1+\left\lVert y\right\rVert)^{-m}\,dy<\infty.

Let the corresponding probability measure be

p⁡(d​y):=ρ⁡(y)​d​y.p(dy):=\rho(y)\,dy.

For each x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, define the associated local probability measure by

upκ​(x)=∫κ⁡(x−y)​p​(𝑑y),πxp,κ​(𝑑y):=κ⁡(x−y)upκ​(x)​p​(𝑑y).u_{p}^{\kappa}(x)=\int\kappa(x-y)\,p(dy),\qquad\pi_{x}^{p,\kappa}(dy):=\frac{\kappa(x-y)}{u_{p}^{\kappa}(x)}\,p(dy). (B.2)

Using polar coordinates and the condition m>dm>d, we obtain

p⁡(‖Y‖>R)=Z−1​|𝕊d−1|​∫R∞rd−1​(1+r)−m​𝑑r.p(\left\lVert Y\right\rVert>R)=Z^{-1}|\mathbb{S}^{d-1}|\int_{R}^{\infty}r^{d-1}(1+r)^{-m}\,dr.

For R≥1R\geq 1,

2−m​r−m≤(1+r)−m≤r−m,2^{-m}r^{-m}\leq(1+r)^{-m}\leq r^{-m},

and integration gives constants 0<c−≤c+<∞0<c_{-}\leq c_{+}<\infty such that

c−​Rd−m≤p⁡(‖Y‖>R)≤c+​Rd−m(R≥1).c_{-}R^{d-m}\leq p(\left\lVert Y\right\rVert>R)\leq c_{+}R^{d-m}\qquad(R\geq 1). (B.3)

Step 3. Fix λ∈(0,λκ)\lambda\in(0,\lambda_{\kappa}), and for j=1,2j=1,2 set

Mjκ:=supx∈ℝd∫ℝd‖y−x‖j​eλ​‖y−x‖​πxp,κ​(𝑑y).M_{j}^{\kappa}:=\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert^{j}e^{\lambda\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert}\,\pi_{x}^{p,\kappa}(dy). (B.4)

We show that these suprema are finite. Fix x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and change variables by y=x+zy=x+z. Then

∫‖y−x‖j​eλ​‖y−x‖​πxp,κ​(𝑑y)=∫ℝd‖z‖j​eλ​‖z‖​κ​(z)​ρ​(x+z)​𝑑z∫ℝdκ⁡(z)​ρ​(x+z)​𝑑z.\int\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert^{j}e^{\lambda\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert}\,\pi_{x}^{p,\kappa}(dy)=\frac{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left\lVert z\right\rVert^{j}e^{\lambda\left\lVert z\right\rVert}\kappa(z)\rho(x+z)\,dz}{\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\kappa(z)\rho(x+z)\,dz}. (B.5)

The inequality

1+‖x+z‖≤1+‖x‖+‖z‖≤(1+‖x‖)​(1+‖z‖)1+\left\lVert x+z\right\rVert\leq 1+\left\lVert x\right\rVert+\left\lVert z\right\rVert\leq(1+\left\lVert x\right\rVert)(1+\left\lVert z\right\rVert)

implies the following lower bound for the density:

ρ⁡(x+z)≥ρ⁡(x)​(1+‖z‖)−m.\rho(x+z)\geq\rho(x)(1+\left\lVert z\right\rVert)^{-m}. (B.6)

Conversely, using

1+‖x‖≤1+‖x+z‖+‖z‖≤(1+‖x+z‖)​(1+‖z‖),1+\left\lVert x\right\rVert\leq 1+\left\lVert x+z\right\rVert+\left\lVert z\right\rVert\leq(1+\left\lVert x+z\right\rVert)(1+\left\lVert z\right\rVert),

we obtain

ρ⁡(x+z)≤ρ⁡(x)​(1+‖z‖)m.\rho(x+z)\leq\rho(x)(1+\left\lVert z\right\rVert)^{m}. (B.7)

Using the density estimates (B.6) and (B.7) in (B.5), we bound the denominator below by

ρ⁡(x)​∫ℝdκ⁡(z)​(1+‖z‖)−m​𝑑z,\rho(x)\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\kappa(z)(1+\left\lVert z\right\rVert)^{-m}\,dz,

and the numerator above by

ρ⁡(x)​∫ℝd‖z‖j​eλ​‖z‖​κ​(z)​(1+‖z‖)m​𝑑z.\rho(x)\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left\lVert z\right\rVert^{j}e^{\lambda\left\lVert z\right\rVert}\kappa(z)(1+\left\lVert z\right\rVert)^{m}\,dz.

The denominator integral is strictly positive and finite, and the numerator integral is finite by (B.1). The common factor ρ⁡(x)\rho(x) cancels, so the resulting bound is uniform in xx. Consequently,

M1κ<∞,M2κ<∞.M_{1}^{\kappa}<\infty,\qquad M_{2}^{\kappa}<\infty. (B.8)

Step 4. Let ϕ:ℝd→ℝ\phi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be a measurable function satisfying

0<Zϕ:=∫eϕ​𝑑p<∞.0<Z_{\phi}:=\int e^{\phi}\,dp<\infty.

Define the tilted law by

qϕ​(d​y):=eϕ⁡(y)Zϕ​p​(d​y).q_{\phi}(dy):=\frac{e^{\phi(y)}}{Z_{\phi}}\,p(dy). (B.9)

In this step, assume that the normalizing constant satisfies 0<Zϕ<∞0<Z_{\phi}<\infty, so that qϕq_{\phi} is well-defined, and that ϕ\phi is globally Lipschitz with Lipschitz constant

L:=Lip⁡(ϕ)≤λ.L:=\operatorname{Lip}(\phi)\leq\lambda.

Fix x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and set

Δx​(y):=ϕ⁡(y)−ϕ⁡(x).\Delta_{x}(y):=\phi(y)-\phi(x).

The global normalizing constant ZϕZ_{\phi} and the common factor eϕ⁡(x)e^{\phi(x)} cancel from the numerator and denominator of the local barycenter formula, yielding

aqϕκ​(x)=∫eΔx​(y)​y​πxp,κ​(𝑑y)∫eΔx​(y)​πxp,κ​(𝑑y).a_{q_{\phi}}^{\kappa}(x)=\frac{\int e^{\Delta_{x}(y)}y\,\pi_{x}^{p,\kappa}(dy)}{\int e^{\Delta_{x}(y)}\,\pi_{x}^{p,\kappa}(dy)}. (B.10)

On the other hand,

apκ​(x)=∫y​πxp,κ​(𝑑y).a_{p}^{\kappa}(x)=\int y\,\pi_{x}^{p,\kappa}(dy). (B.11)

The difference between (B.10) and (B.11) can be written as

aqϕκ​(x)−apκ​(x)=∫(eΔx​(y)−1)​(y−apκ​(x))​πxp,κ​(𝑑y)∫eΔx​(y)​πxp,κ​(𝑑y).a_{q_{\phi}}^{\kappa}(x)-a_{p}^{\kappa}(x)=\frac{\int(e^{\Delta_{x}(y)}-1)\bigl(y-a_{p}^{\kappa}(x)\bigr)\,\pi_{x}^{p,\kappa}(dy)}{\int e^{\Delta_{x}(y)}\,\pi_{x}^{p,\kappa}(dy)}. (B.12)

The Lipschitz condition on ϕ\phi gives

|Δx​(y)|≤L⁡‖y−x‖.|\Delta_{x}(y)|\leq L\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert.

Using this fact, Jensen’s inequality, and M1κ<∞M_{1}^{\kappa}<\infty from (B.8), we obtain the following lower bound for the denominator:

∫eΔx​(y)πxp,κ(dy)≥∫e−L​‖y−x‖πxp,κ(dy)≥exp(−L∫‖y−x‖πxp,κ(dy))≥e−λ​M1κ.\int e^{\Delta_{x}(y)}\,\pi_{x}^{p,\kappa}(dy)\geq\int e^{-L\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert}\,\pi_{x}^{p,\kappa}(dy)\geq\exp\!\left(-L\int\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert\,\pi_{x}^{p,\kappa}(dy)\right)\geq e^{-\lambda M_{1}^{\kappa}}. (B.13)

Moreover,

‖apκ​(x)−x‖=‖∫(y−x)​πxp,κ​(𝑑y)‖≤∫‖y−x‖​πxp,κ​(𝑑y)≤M1κ,\left\lVert a_{p}^{\kappa}(x)-x\right\rVert=\left\|\int(y-x)\,\pi_{x}^{p,\kappa}(dy)\right\|\leq\int\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert\,\pi_{x}^{p,\kappa}(dy)\leq M_{1}^{\kappa},

and hence the triangle inequality gives

‖y−apκ​(x)‖≤‖y−x‖+M1κ.\left\lVert y-a_{p}^{\kappa}(x)\right\rVert\leq\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert+M_{1}^{\kappa}.

Also, for every t≥0t\geq 0, |eL​t−1|≤L​t​eL​t|e^{Lt}-1|\leq Lt\,e^{Lt}. Therefore

∫|eΔx​(y)−1|​‖y−apκ​(x)‖​πxp,κ​(dy)\displaystyle\int|e^{\Delta_{x}(y)}-1|\,\left\lVert y-a_{p}^{\kappa}(x)\right\rVert\,\pi_{x}^{p,\kappa}(dy) (B.14)
≤∫(eL​‖y−x‖−1)​(‖y−x‖+M1κ)​πxp,κ​(dy)\displaystyle\leq\int(e^{L\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert}-1)\bigl(\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert+M_{1}^{\kappa}\bigr)\,\pi_{x}^{p,\kappa}(dy)
≤L​∫‖y−x‖2​eL​‖y−x‖​πxp,κ​(dy)+L​M1κ​∫‖y−x‖​eL​‖y−x‖​πxp,κ​(dy)\displaystyle\leq L\int\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert^{2}e^{L\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert}\,\pi_{x}^{p,\kappa}(dy)+LM_{1}^{\kappa}\int\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert e^{L\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert}\,\pi_{x}^{p,\kappa}(dy)
≤L⁡(M2κ+(M1κ)2).\displaystyle\leq L\bigl(M_{2}^{\kappa}+(M_{1}^{\kappa})^{2}\bigr).

The last inequality in (B.14) uses the condition L≤λL\leq\lambda, which gives eL​‖y−x‖≤eλ​‖y−x‖e^{L\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert}\leq e^{\lambda\left\lVert y-x\right\rVert}, together with the uniform bounds M1κM_{1}^{\kappa} and M2κM_{2}^{\kappa} from (B.8).

Combining the denominator lower bound (B.13) and the numerator upper bound (B.14), we obtain

‖aqϕκ​(x)−apκ​(x)‖≤eλ​M1κ​(M2κ+(M1κ)2)​L.\left\lVert a_{q_{\phi}}^{\kappa}(x)-a_{p}^{\kappa}(x)\right\rVert\leq e^{\lambda M_{1}^{\kappa}}\bigl(M_{2}^{\kappa}+(M_{1}^{\kappa})^{2}\bigr)\,L. (B.15)

The right-hand side is independent of xx. Hence there exists a constant

C=C⁡(κ,λ,p)<∞C=C(\kappa,\lambda,p)<\infty

for which the global estimate

‖aqϕκ−apκ‖L∞​(ℝd)≤C​L\|a_{q_{\phi}}^{\kappa}-a_{p}^{\kappa}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\leq C\,L (B.16)

holds.

Step 5. Choose a Lipschitz cutoff function ψ:[0,∞)→[0,1]\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,1] satisfying

ψ⁡(r)=0(r≤1),ψ⁡(r)=1(r≥2),Lip⁡(ψ)≤1.\psi(r)=0\quad(r\leq 1),\qquad\psi(r)=1\quad(r\geq 2),\qquad\operatorname{Lip}(\psi)\leq 1.

Define

tn:=p⁡(‖Y‖>2​n),αn:=−log⁡tn,ϕn​(x):=αn​ψ​(‖x‖/n),t_{n}:=p(\left\lVert Y\right\rVert>2n),\qquad\alpha_{n}:=-\log t_{n},\qquad\phi_{n}(x):=\alpha_{n}\,\psi(\left\lVert x\right\rVert/n),

qn:=qϕn.q_{n}:=q_{\phi_{n}}.

1≤Zϕn=∫eϕn​𝑑p≤eαn<∞,1\leq Z_{\phi_{n}}=\int e^{\phi_{n}}\,dp\leq e^{\alpha_{n}}<\infty,

so each probability measure qnq_{n} is well-defined. By construction,

Lip⁡(ϕn)≤αn/n.\operatorname{Lip}(\phi_{n})\leq\alpha_{n}/n.

Applying (B.3) with R=2​nR=2n gives

c−​(2​n)d−m≤tn≤c+​(2​n)d−m,c_{-}(2n)^{d-m}\leq t_{n}\leq c_{+}(2n)^{d-m},

and taking logarithms yields

αn=−log⁡tn=(m−d)​log⁡n+O⁡(1).\alpha_{n}=-\log t_{n}=(m-d)\log n+O(1).

Therefore, as n→∞n\to\infty,

αnn→0.\frac{\alpha_{n}}{n}\to 0.

Recall the fixed λ∈(0,λκ)\lambda\in(0,\lambda_{\kappa}) from Step 4. For all sufficiently large nn, Lip⁡(ϕn)≤λ\operatorname{Lip}(\phi_{n})\leq\lambda, and applying (B.16) with ϕ=ϕn\phi=\phi_{n} gives

‖aqnκ−apκ‖L∞​(ℝd)≤C​Lip⁡(ϕn)→0.\|a_{q_{n}}^{\kappa}-a_{p}^{\kappa}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\leq C\,\operatorname{Lip}(\phi_{n})\to 0.

Thus the global bound on the drift field converges to zero:

‖Vp,qnκ‖L∞​(ℝd)=‖apκ−aqnκ‖L∞​(ℝd)→0.\|V_{p,q_{n}}^{\kappa}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}=\|a_{p}^{\kappa}-a_{q_{n}}^{\kappa}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d})}\to 0.

Step 6. On the set {‖x‖>2n}\{\left\lVert x\right\rVert>2n\}, one has ϕn​(x)=αn\phi_{n}(x)=\alpha_{n}, and hence

eϕn​(x)=eαn=tn−1.e^{\phi_{n}(x)}=e^{\alpha_{n}}=t_{n}^{-1}. (B.17)

Zn:=∫eϕn​𝑑p.Z_{n}:=\int e^{\phi_{n}}\,dp.

qn​(‖X‖>2​n)=tn−1​p​(‖X‖>2​n)Zn=1Zn.q_{n}(\left\lVert X\right\rVert>2n)=\frac{t_{n}^{-1}p(\left\lVert X\right\rVert>2n)}{Z_{n}}=\frac{1}{Z_{n}}. (B.18)

Zn≤p⁡(Bn​(0))+eαn​p​(Bn​(0)c)≤1+tn−1​p​(‖X‖>n).Z_{n}\leq p(B_{n}(0))+e^{\alpha_{n}}p(B_{n}(0)^{c})\leq 1+t_{n}^{-1}p(\left\lVert X\right\rVert>n).

Applying (B.3) at R=nR=n and R=2​nR=2n to estimate the ratio of the two tail probabilities, we obtain

p⁡(‖X‖>n)tn=p⁡(‖X‖>n)p⁡(‖X‖>2​n)≤c+​nd−mc−​(2​n)d−m=c+c−​ 2m−d.\frac{p(\left\lVert X\right\rVert>n)}{t_{n}}=\frac{p(\left\lVert X\right\rVert>n)}{p(\left\lVert X\right\rVert>2n)}\leq\frac{c_{+}n^{d-m}}{c_{-}(2n)^{d-m}}=\frac{c_{+}}{c_{-}}\,2^{m-d}.

Hence

Zn≤1+c+c−​ 2m−d=:1+C∗(∀n).Z_{n}\leq 1+\frac{c_{+}}{c_{-}}\,2^{m-d}=:1+C_{\ast}\qquad(\forall n).

Consequently, we obtain a uniform lower bound on the tail probability of qnq_{n}:

qn​(‖X‖>2​n)=1Zn≥11+C∗=:ε0>0.q_{n}(\left\lVert X\right\rVert>2n)=\frac{1}{Z_{n}}\geq\frac{1}{1+C_{\ast}}=:\varepsilon_{0}>0.

Thus, for any fixed R>0R>0, choosing n>R/2n>R/2 gives

qn​(BR​(0)c)≥qn​(‖X‖>2​n)≥ε0.q_{n}(B_{R}(0)^{c})\geq q_{n}(\left\lVert X\right\rVert>2n)\geq\varepsilon_{0}.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
